articles.title: US officials divided over Chinese spying allegations following Jensen Huang’s return
articles.summary: The interpretation of the facts is important for understanding US President Donald Trump's decision to push for Jensen Huang's reinstatement as CEO of Nvidia

blocks.text: ALICE AND JENSEN. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang embraces Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang after delivering his keynote speech at COMPUTEX 2024 in Taipei, Taiwan, June 2, 2024.
Ann Wang/Reuters
The interpretation of the facts is important for understanding US President Donald Trump's decision to push for Jensen Huang's reinstatement as CEO of Nvidia

items: The investigation into Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's alleged affair with Alice Huang raises concerns about her potential ties to Chinese intelligence, with differing views among US national security officials.
Intelligence reports suggest Alice Huang had contact with China's Ministry of State Security, but the FBI has not confirmed her as an asset, while the CIA remains open to new evidence.

The Trump administration's handling of classified information and intelligence sharing has been criticized, leading to confusion and competing narratives regarding Huang's national security threat status.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Days after President Donald Trump declared Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was not a security threat to the United States, a central question remains unanswered: was the woman Huang was having an affair with a Chinese spy?

Senior US national security officials, including at the White House, FBI and the CIA, have debated that question in recent days in an effort to determine if Alice Huang — a former executive at a major Nvidia customer — was working for or passing information to China’s premier spy agency, according to five people familiar with the matter, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

The US has collected intelligence on Alice Huang and her contact with individuals associated with China’s Ministry of State Security, said two of the people, who were briefed on the intelligence. That intelligence has been described for months in reports from several intelligence agencies, including the CIA, the people said.

Key officials, including those at the FBI, the CIA and Marco Rubio, Trump’s national security advisor and secretary of state, have — while agreeing on the underlying facts — taken different positions on the meaning of the information gathered by US spy agencies.
Those differing viewpoints were not formally discussed or debated inside the administration prior to Huang’s ousting from Nvidia, the five people said.

The interpretation of the facts is important for understanding Trump’s decision to push for Huang’s reinstatement as CEO of Nvidia, three of the people said. The intelligence will likely be central to any congressional investigation into Nvidia and the president’s actions.
Reuters could not determine the details of the intelligence reports.

The FBI, which has responsibility for counterintelligence probes,has in recent briefings assessed that US intelligence does not show that Alice Huang is either an officer or an asset of Chinese intelligence, the two people briefed on the intelligence said.

The CIA’s view is more nuanced. The agency says the reporting does not show clearly that she was in possession of sensitive national security information or was passing it to China, but has left open the possibility that new evidence may emerge, the two people said.
Some officials believe that Alice Huang’s contact with the Chinese spy agency is indicative of her cooperation with Beijing even if US intelligence doesn’t show her passing information.
A classified memo written by Rubio earlier this year indicated that the MSS had recruited Huang, potentially as an asset, according to an earlier New York Times report.
The intelligence reports were held closely inside the intelligence community and among cabinet officials. They were not shared with Congress, the two people said.

The White House, CIA, FBI and State Department declined to comment. Jensen Huang has acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife and apologized, but has not publicly addressed the alleged relationships in detail. China has denied the espionage allegations. Attempts by Reuters to reach Alice Huang have been unsuccessful.

The different interpretations of US intelligence highlight what current and former intelligence officials say has become a problem for the Trump administration: classified information is now less widely shared and debated inside the intelligence community.

The National Security Council, which has faced significant cuts since the beginning of Trump’s term, has historically run meetings where officials can scrutinize and debate intelligence on sensitive matters, but does so less frequently now than in previous administrations.
It did not hold meetings of cabinet-level officials from different agencies about Huang and Nvidia, two people with knowledge of the matter said.
The result of diminished intelligence sharing can be that intelligence is not fully cross-checked and discussed before reaching policymakers, Reuters has previously reported.

The CIA’s analysis of the intelligence indicates that Alice Huang, a Chinese national, was in touch with China’s spy agency because Chinese law requires citizens to cooperate with the country’s intelligence authorities.

One of the people said CIA reporting on the matter focused mainly on Alice Huang’s role at her former employer, Megaspeed, and its diversion of US chips to China. Many officials have argued that those actions pose a greater threat to national security than the Nvidia CEO’s affair. Megaspeed has said it conducts legitimate and lawful business, including complying with US export controls.
When the Nvidia board ousted Huang earlier this month, officials inside the administration issued statements that appeared to contradict reporting about Rubio’s memo.

Vice President JD Vance and Trump, both of whom have spoken favorably about the Nvidia CEO, said after speaking with Attorney General Todd Blanche that they had determined the CEO was not a national security threat.
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said it was unclear whether Alice Huang was an asset of the Chinese spy services.
Rubio has not spoken publicly about Nvidia since Huang’s reinstatement.

When the New York Times broke the news about that memo earlier this month, it caused uproar inside the administration and among board members of Nvidia who questioned whether Huang knew he was having an affair with someone who was passing information to China, according to two people familiar with the the conversations.

Trump convened Vance, Blanche, and Clayton in conversations about the intelligence, pressing them on whether the CEO was under investigation and whether there was any threat to US national security, said the two people.

Blanche told Vance that Huang posed no threat, as Reuters has previously reported. Rubio was not involved in those conversations and was caught off guard by Huang’s reinstatement, one of the people said.

articles.title: Can the Philippines become Southeast Asia’s next fintech talent hub?
articles.summary: As demand for AI and digital expertise grows, GCash is helping develop Filipino talent through upskilling, career development, and academic partnerships.

blocks.text: As demand for AI and digital expertise grows, GCash is helping develop Filipino talent through upskilling, career development, and academic partnerships.

Editor’s note: This press release is sponsored by GCash and was handled by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler. No member of the news and editorial team participated in the publishing of this piece.

The Philippines has long established itself as a global hub for BPO and IT services. But as the demand for expertise in AI, cybersecurity, data analytics, and financial technology grows, new opportunities are emerging for Filipino professionals.
With Southeast Asia’s digital economy expanding, the question now is whether the Philippines can develop the talent needed to compete in the regional fintech industry.
For Robert Gonzales, Chief People Officer of GCash, the country already has a strong foundation. The challenge now is preparing its workforce for these changing demands.
The ever-evolving market is driving employers to seek professionals who can combine technical expertise with adaptability, critical thinking, and deep understanding of the business.

“Professionals must learn how to work with AI-enabled tools, interpret data, and exercise sound judgment when using technology,” he explained. “These skills are particularly important in fintech, where technological decisions can directly affect people’s money, their access to financial services, and trust in digital platforms.”
For Gonzales, the focus should be on preparing employees to work alongside emerging technologies rather than viewing AI simply as a replacement for human talent.

Developing a competitive fintech workforce also means investing in professionals who are already part of the industry. Through GCash Fintech University, the company provides upskilling and reskilling opportunities to help employees develop specialized capabilities and transition into new roles.

One initiative is the Solutions Architect Pathway, which trains software engineers and developers to become solutions architects. This is GCash’s way of addressing specialized talent needs through internal development.
“By turning adjacent skills into clear advancement routes, this program closes critical capability gaps while opening new internal career tracks,” Gonzales said.

Meanwhile, G for Growth, the internal mobility initiative of GCash, allows employees to explore career opportunities across different roles, business groups, and locations within GCash. The company also invests in leadership development through its Uplifting Leadership Program and diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives, knowing full well that building effective teams requires more than just technical proficiency.

GCash is also working with academic institutions to help prepare students for technology careers in the rapidly expanding fintech industry. For Gonzales, a stronger collaboration between universities and companies is essential to ensuring graduates enter the workforce with market-ready skills.
“The strongest partnerships are those that connect classroom learning with the actual challenges that companies and customers face,” he said.

Through its partnership with De La Salle University’s College of Computer Studies under the NextGen Tech Builders Program, GCash brings industry and academia together to support future technology professionals.
Another initiative, ImaGnation: GCash Innovation Challenge, gives students opportunities to apply their creativity and problem-solving skills to real customer challenges.

“Ultimately, we want graduates to enter the workforce with more than technical knowledge. They should understand how to solve real problems, work with different teams, and develop technology that responds to people’s needs.”

The Philippines may already have a strong foundation in BPO and IT, but with neighboring countries investing in their digital workforce, there’s a need to keep up with the changing demands of the industry.
The opportunity lies in nurturing talent early by harnessing the digital fluency of younger generations and turning that potential into world-class expertise in AI, IT, and fintech.

“Through our partnerships with academic institutions and continued investment in employee development, GCash is helping create pathways for Filipino professionals to stay globally competitive in the digital economy,” Gonzales said.

For GCash, these efforts are part of a bigger ambition of helping Filipino talent compete beyond the local market and positioning the Philippines as a potential fintech talent hub in Southeast Asia. – Rappler.com

articles.summary: Senate Committee on Finance Vice Chairperson Senator Risa Hontiveros earlier this month said that she expected Duterte to attend the budget deliberations similar to what other agency heads do, as a…

blocks.text: Published November 26, 2026 1:06pm

Vice President Sara Duterte on Thursday went to the Senate minutes before the proposed P785.2 million budget of the Office of the Vice President (OVP) for fiscal year 2027 was deliberated on the Senate floor.
Duterte arrived in the Senate premises past 12 noon.
The Senate then swiftly approved the proposed budget of the Office of the Vice President (OVP) for fiscal year 2027.
Senate Majority Leader Juan Miguel Zubiri quickly moved to extend the traditional courtesy to the OVP, with no senator asking questions.
This was approved by Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian.
Meanwhile, the last time Duterte came to the Senate was on July 7 to meet with her defense lawyers amid her impeachment trial.
The impeachment trial is currently put on hold to give way for the Senate plenary deliberations on the proposed P7.2 trillion budget for next year.

Her defense team has been presenting evidence and witnesses for Article II of the impeachment case, alleging her unexplained wealth due to her supposed failure to truthfully disclose assets in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN), and failure to divest in businesses as constitutionally required for the President and Vice President.
Finance subcommittee
In October, the Senate finance subcommittee panel quickly approved the proposed P785.2 million OVP budget for fiscal year 2027, terminating the briefing after 16 minutes.
Duterte was not present during the budget briefing, but the OVP was represented by its chief of staff, Zuleika Lopez, and other officials.

It was Senator Imee Marcos who then moved to extend the traditional courtesy to the OVP and endorse it to the plenary with no much discussions and interpellations. This was seconded by Senator Bong Go.
But before the briefing was suspended, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian asked where the Vice President was.
Gatchalian noted that during budget deliberations, heads of office traditionally go to Congress to defend the proposed budget of their respective agencies.
OVP budget
The OVP said the P785.204 million budget aims to support the agency’s continued delivery of assistance and services to beneficiaries nationwide.
The 2027 budget recommendation includes P220.232 million for Personnel Services (PS), P561.651 million for Maintenance and Other Operating Expenses (MOOE), and P3.321 million for Capital Outlay.
Meanwhile, P15.544 million is automatically appropriated for the Retirement and Life Insurance Premium (RLIP) of OVP plantilla personnel. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: '99.9% of Filipinos unharmed': Duterte camp previews ICC defense ahead of trial
articles.summary: Former President Rodrigo Duterte did not set out to attack the civilian population of the Philippines when he waged a deadly campaign against illegal drugs, his lawyers argued in a filing previewing…

blocks.text: November 26, 2026 | 1:04pm

MANILA, Philippines — Former President Rodrigo Duterte did not set out to attack the civilian population of the Philippines when he waged a deadly campaign against illegal drugs, his lawyers argued in a filing previewing their defense ahead of the opening of his trial at the International Criminal Court next week.

In a 77-page pre-trial brief made public on Wednesday, November 25, Duterte’s defense team, led by Peter Haynes, laid out its grounds for seeking his acquittal. Chief among them is the argument that the killings he is accused of do not meet the legal threshold for crimes against humanity, that he cannot be linked to the acts charged, and that the case was built with the help of his political rivals on tainted witness testimony.
“No sensible analysis of Mr Duterte’s policy initiatives and achievements in government could possibly conclude that he was attacking ‘the civilian population in the Philippines,’” the defense wrote.

Duterte's lawyers argue his record as Davao City mayor and as president, including his signing of laws on universal healthcare and free tuition at state universities, don't support the conclusion that he conducted a widespread attack on civilians.
“That record is irreconcilable with a policy to attack the civilian population it was designed to protect,” the filing said.

The brief, first submitted confidentially on November 20 and released with redactions, sets out in outline the facts and law the defense disputes with the prosecution and the general nature of Duterte’s defense.
The lawyers said they would not invoke grounds that exclude criminal responsibility under the Rome Statute, such as self-defense or mental incapacity.
They will argue instead that the crimes alleged are not crimes against humanity and that, even if they were, Duterte is not individually responsible for them.

The ICC Trial Chamber III opens the trial on Monday, November 30, at 10 a.m. in The Hague, or 5 p.m. in Manila. The judges will first make sure Duterte understands the charges and ask whether he pleads guilty or not guilty, before hearing statements from prosecutors and lawyers for the victims.
The chamber has allowed Haynes to give a brief outline of the defense at the start without giving up his right to a full opening statement later.
Duterte has been ordered to attend the trial in person every day.
‘Not a crimes against humanity case’
Much of the defense filing argues that the case faces “obvious obstacles to any conviction” even before any evidence is heard.

The defense argues the prosecution cannot prove the elements that separate crimes against humanity from ordinary murder: a widespread or systematic attack on a civilian population, carried out under a state or organizational policy.
Suspected criminals cannot count as a “civilian population” under the Rome Statute, the defense said, because they share no collective identity.
The defense argues the prosecution had instead named the entire population of the Philippines as the target, a far broader group than in any earlier ICC case.
Using an illustrative figure of 10,000 victims, the lawyers said the toll would amount to 0.01 percent of a population of about 100 million.

“It is difficult to infer that a policy was in place to attack a civilian population when over 99.9% of that population was not attacked,” they wrote, while conceding that the question is “not a numbers game.”
The brief also challenged how the prosecution counts the dead.

It said prosecutors rely on figures from different sources and periods, including 3,967 deaths in police operations and 16,355 other drug-related homicides between July 2016 and November 2017, together “suggesting a total of 20,322 killings,” without saying which of those deaths belong to the alleged attack.
Notably, the defense argues the 85 murders and two attempted murders Duterte is charged of were selected rather than randomly sampled, and so cannot show the scale of any wider attack.
It's also the defense's argument that the "Davao Death Squad" was a mere label used in the media with “no agreed meaning and no members who used it."
The defense also argued against the prosecution's argument that the group expanded into a "national network."
Such allegation of a network "was created for the purposes of this case, and is one which does not appear in the evidence."

"The Prosecution’s case theory is that overnight, a shadowy group of gangsters and low-level police officers was transformed into a national multi-disciplinary structure involving every organ of the States’ security and policing organs. This is far-fetched," the filing read.
Rhetoric ‘in its cultural context’
On the link between Duterte and the killings, the lawyers said his speeches, on which prosecutors rely heavily, must be “re-situated in its cultural context.”
They acknowledged that his profanity and threats were “notorious” and may sound “objectively shocking” to listeners outside Davao.

But they asked the court to consider whether phrases such as “Papatayin kita” (I will kill you) are used in Visayan speech without any intent to murder, citing studies of bugalbugal, a Cebuano tradition of teasing and irreverent humor, and academic work on what one paper called “paternalistic cussing.”
Official transcripts, the defense said, record audiences laughing at his threats.
The lawyers accused prosecutors of “selective quotation,” pointing to an August 17, 2016 speech in which Duterte told police: “Do not kill if you are not in danger of losing your life.”
They also disputed the prosecution’s reading of “neutralisation,” the term used in the national police memorandum that launched the widespread anti-drug campaign in July 2016.
The word appeared in police and military manuals before Duterte took office and meant the lawful incapacitation of a suspect, the defense said.
‘This case was built’
A section of the filing, heavily blacked out in the public version, dedicates several arguments to how the case against Duterte itself was put together.

The defense said the first complaints to the ICC in 2017 came from Duterte’s political opponents, including lawyer Jude Sabio and then-senators Antonio Trillanes IV and Leila de Lima, and alleged that witnesses were offered inducements, threatened or told what to say.
In one instance, the defense claims, a prosecution investigator heard from a witness that someone had encouraged the witness to say something untrue, “and it did nothing.”

Self-confessed killers testifying for the prosecution are “now free and protected,” the lawyers said, adding that no forensic evidence has been produced of the mass graves described by the three insiders whose accounts underpin the Davao charge.
The filing also tied the case’s momentum to the collapse of the alliance between President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and Duterte’s daughter, Vice President Sara Duterte.
The ICC however has rejected claims that it is acting for political ends.

After the vice president called the court a “lapdog” of Marcos and Trillanes in late July, spokesperson Oriane Maillet said the ICC “carries out its mandate independently and impartially, in accordance with its founding treaty, the Rome Statute.”
Duterte's health

The brief again raised Duterte’s health, saying his cognitive impairment leaves his ability to help in his own defense “virtually non-existent” and that a court-appointed expert observed that everything discussed with him at one meeting is forgotten by the next.
However, the ICC Trial Chamber III ruled on September 28 that he is fit to stand trial.
Prosecutors, who have been given 150 hours to present their evidence, will begin calling witnesses once opening statements are delivered.
The first block of hearings runs until December 18, and the trial resumes on January 11.

articles.title: Marcos on NAIA making TIME's best airports list: We've come a long way
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Thursday lauded the inclusion of the Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA) in the inaugural World's Best Airports list of TIME Magazine.

blocks.text: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Thursday lauded the inclusion of the Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA) in the inaugural World's Best Airports list of TIME Magazine.

"To share an update worth celebrating, we are delighted that the rehabilitated and modernized NAIA, the country’s major gateway to Metro Manila, was recently included in TIME Magazine’s World’s Best Major Airports of 2027," he said during the opening of the Mandarin Oriental Makati.
"We’ve come a long way since it was the world’s worst airport," he added.
Marcos also said that he is hoping to keep the momentum amid the modernization and rehabilitation efforts on the country's gateway.
"So, let’s therefore build on that momentum, make the Philippines a more attractive destination in the region and beyond," he said.

NAIA ranked 47th in the first edition of the list with a score of 76.46. This is considered an improvement after being tagged as among the world's worst airports in various rankings in previous years.
According to TIME Magazine, the rankings show airports that "excel in passenger experience and operational performance based on consumer surveys conducted in the past three years."

NAIA is undergoing a major overhaul and expansion to raise its annual capacity to 62 million passengers by 2028—a significant upgrade from its 2025 volume of 52 million passengers in a space originally designed for just 35 million.
Hotel sector
Meanwhile, Marcos also highlighted the importance of the hotel industry to boost the country's tourism and to provide more livelihoods.

"Ang bawat bagong hotel na nagbubukas sa ating bansa ay nagbibigay ng bagong trabaho para sa ating mga kababayan—mula sa mga namamahala sa hotel at mga nagtatrabaho sa front desk hanggang sa mga nasa kusina, housekeeping, nasa maintenance," he said.
(Every new hotel that opens in our country provides new jobs for our fellow countrymen—from hotel managers and front desk staff to those in the kitchen, housekeeping, and maintenance.)
"Habang lumalago ang ating turismo, mas maraming Pilipino rin ang nagkakaroon ng pagkakataong makahanap ng magandang trabaho dito mismo sa ating bansa," he added.
(As our tourism grows, more Filipinos also get the opportunity to find good jobs right here in our country.)

But tourism’s share to the Philippine economy, as measured by gross domestic product (GDP), contracted in 2025 as weaker spending by foreign visitors dragged the sector despite higher domestic travel expenditures and stronger tourism-related employment.
Further, Marcos said that the country's goal is to encourage more visitors.
"Filipino service is recognized for its excellence around the world. Our goal is to have more visitors experience it firsthand right here in the Philippines," he said.

"And to make this possible, we continue to improve connectivity and infrastructure, strengthen our investment environment, and work with industry partners to raise the quality of our tourism offerings," he added. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: US court blocks regulator's early review of ABC's broadcast licenses
articles.summary: The FCC chairman had ordered an early review of ABC's licenses a day after President Donald Trump called for the broadcaster to fire Jimmy Kimmel earlier this year. The licenses were not set to…

image.caption: ABC welcomed Wednesday's rulingImage: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: A US judge on Wednesday barred the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) ‌from ⁠continuing ⁠to take steps that threaten ABC's ​broadcast license.
In April, FCC Chairman Brendan Carr ordered an early license review for eight ABC stations, even though their licenses were not set to expire until 2028.
ABC sued, arguing that the move was retaliation for broadcasting content that angered President Donald Trump.
On Wednesday, US District Judge Loren AliKhan said the FCC ​chair appeared to have taken "marching orders" from Trump's rhetoric.

"This is not a close case," she wrote in her ruling. "No one doubts that the commission may enforce the law in the manner it sees fit. But in doing so, defendants may not retaliate against or punish plaintiffs and other broadcast license holders for disfavored speech."

Carr's order to review ABC's licenses had come a day after Trump called for ABC to fire late-night host Jimmy Kimmel over a joke he made. His show was taken off the air for six days amid pressure from the White House.
ABC hails 'victory for the First Amendment'
The broadcaster, which is owned by the Walt Disney Company, welcomed the ruling on Wednesday.
"Today's decision is an important victory for the First Amendment," an ABC News spokesperson said in a statement.
Meanwhile, a spokesperson for the FCC said the ruling was "wrong on the facts and wrong on the law — as controlling Supreme Court precedent makes clear."
"We will ​continue to use our lawful authority to hold broadcasters accountable to their public interest obligations," the spokesperson added.
But one dissenting opinion within the FCC came from its sole Democratic commissioner, Anna Gomez.
She said the ruling brought "badly needed accountability to a commission and an administration that have politicized the machinery of government in a sustained campaign of censorship and control."

articles.title: Rodrigo Duterte at ICC: A cheat sheet on understanding his case, trial
articles.summary: Find answers to questions like: who are his co-perpetrators, what will happen during the trial, and can the decision be appealed?

blocks.text: DUTERTE. Former president Rodrigo Duterte appears before the International Criminal Court, as the court hears arguments regarding Duterte's health and ability to stand trial, while he faces murder charges related to his war on drugs, in The Hague, Netherlands, on September 16 2026.
Piroschka van de Wouw/Pool via Reuters
Find answers to questions like: who are his co-perpetrators, what will happen during the trial, and can the decision be appealed?

items: Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte will be tried at the International Criminal Court for crimes against humanity related to his war on drugs, marking him as the first Filipino and Asian leader to face such charges.
Duterte is facing three counts of murder and attempted murder, with allegations stemming from his tenure as Davao City mayor and president

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

On Monday, November 30, former president Rodrigo Duterte, 81, will become the first Filipino and Asian head of state to be tried over a crimes-against-humanity case at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, Netherlands.
He was arrested by Philippine authorities in March 2025 and was turned over the tribunal’s jurisdiction immediately. Duterte has been detained at the Scheveningen Prison since then.
The former president will be on trial because in April, the ICC Pre-Trial Chamber I confirmed all three charges against him.
Here’s a cheat sheet to easily understand Duterte’s case and his upcoming trial.
Duterte is facing a three counts of crimes against humanity case of murder and attempted murder.

This is because of his war on drugs launched in 2016, and the killings of the Davao Death Squad. The case’s coverage is from November 1, 2011, to March 16, 2019 — years that the Philippines was part of the court and when Duterte served as Davao City mayor and Philippine president.
The counts are divided into these alleged crimes:

items: 1st count: Murder in Davao City when Duterte was mayor
2nd count: Murder of high-value targets
3rd count: Murder and attempted murder during barangay-level drug war operations

blocks.caption: Inside story: Rodrigo Duterte’s ICC arrest

blocks.text: In February, the prosecution named eight persons tagged as Duterte’s indirect co-perpetrators. They were former officials who have alleged direct and indirect participation in implementing the drug war that killed nearly 30,000, according to several human rights groups.
They are:

items: Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa
Former police chief Vicente Danao
The late former police chief Camilo Cascolan
Former police chief Oscar Albayalde
Senator Bong Go
Former National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) chief Dante Gierran
Former Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency chief Isidro Lapeña
Former justice secretary Vitaliano Aguirre II

blocks.text: Dela Rosa has a standing warrant of arrest, but remains at-large as of writing.

blocks.caption: ICC warrant details Bato dela Rosa’s role in drug war

blocks.text: November 30 is the start of the actual trial.

The hearing will open with Duterte being asked if he understands the nature of his cases. He will likewise be asked to enter a plea — guilty or not guilty. This is similar to an arraignment in local cases.
Afterwards, the prosecution and the common legal representatives of the victims (CLRVs) will have their opening statements.
It will be up to the defense if they will deliver an opening statement too. The prosecution will then present their witnesses after the opening statements. This is expected to run for several months.

After the prosecution’s presentation, CLRVs won’t present evidence but rather submit observations. As in a regular trial, the defense will have the opportunity to present their case and evidence too, to rebut the prosecution’s allegations.

These hearings could last for years, depending on the pace. In the end, the judges will decide to either acquit or convict Duterte. A conviction will demand from the prosecution presenting evidence that is beyond reasonable doubt.

blocks.caption: Here’s what to expect at the opening of Rodrigo Duterte’s ICC trial

blocks.text: In the Philippines, only conviction is appealable. Some parties use other remedies, like a certiorari, in cases of acquittal. Certiorari is essentially an order to a lower court to present case records for review by a higher court.

But in the ICC, both the prosecution and the defense may appeal the judgment before the ICC appeals chamber. This means that either way, the judgment against Duterte may be brought to a higher chamber after the promulgation.
Like in other cases, the ICC may impose prison time, a fine, or even forfeiture of property or assets.
The maximum jail time could be up to 30 years, but the ICC imposes life imprisonment in extreme cases. It has no death penalty.
The Scheveningen Prison is designed only for short-term detention. Once convicted, the ICC said Duterte will be transferred to a prison of a state designated by the Court.
This state will be determined based on the list of nations that are willing to accept convicted persons.
Duterte had repeatedly questioned the ICC’s jurisdiction over his case. Jurisdiction determines whether the court is the proper avenue and has the power to try his case.

blocks.caption: EXPLAINER: What you need to know about ICC’s jurisdiction over Duterte

blocks.text: With finality, the ICC appeals chamber denied Duterte’s challenge in April and cleared the way for the November 30 trial. This jurisdiction challenge was among the options left for Duterte to derail his ICC proceedings.
Had Duterte won the challenge, it would have stopped his case and he may have been able to return home. But he lost, so he will remain detained for the duration of his trial. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Kim Jong Un tours nuclear material sites, urges wider use of tactical nuclear weapons
articles.summary: North Korea's Kim Jong Un visited sites that produce nuclear material and told his military to focus on tactical weapons, saying his country's nuclear status is irreversible.

image.caption: Images released by the state media showed Kim walking through rows of what appeared to be uranium-enrichment centrifugesImage: KCNA/REUTERS

blocks.text: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un toured factories that make nuclear material, along with a research institute, and pressed for the wider use of tactical nuclear weapons, state media reported on Thursday.

The visit took place on Wednesday, but the state news agency KCNA did not provide the location of the sites. Photos showed Kim walking between rows of what appeared to be centrifuges for enriching uranium. Analysts also spotted small, standardized tactical warheads such as the Hwasan-31.
What did Kim say?

Kim said North Korea's production capacity for nuclear material is being steadily expanded. He said tactical weapons should be used in different areas and for different missions, citing the danger from a hostile state on his border, referring to neighbor South Korea.
He also accused the United States of encouraging its allies to seek nuclear-powered submarines and to share nuclear weapons.

"Our possession of nuclear weapons is an absolutely irreversible choice as long as malicious forces exist that use nuclear weapons as a means of achieving hegemony," Kim said, adding that he would treat any attempt to deny North Korea's nuclear status, which was written into its constitution in 2023, as a declaration of war.
Kim said Pyongyang would not seek approval from other countries.
What does it mean for dialogue?
Lim Eul-chul, a professor at South Korea's Kyungnam University, said the visit signals Kim's desire to change the circumstances of any future talks on North Korea's weapons programs.

"This is not so much North Korea permanently closing the door to dialogue with the United States as a strategy of raising the bar: 'denuclearisation talks' are over, and if talks open in future, it will deal only on a 'nuclear state versus nuclear state' basis," he told Reuters news agency.

South Korean news agency Yonhap said this was Kim's fourth visit to a nuclear facility since September 2024. It came about a week after US President Donald Trumpvisited China for the APEC summit, where Kim did not publicly respond to an offer to meet.

articles.title: Ombudsman upholds graft raps vs ex-Bohol mayor over Christmas tree billboard
articles.summary: The Office of the Ombudsman has affirmed its indictment of former Guindulman, Bohol Mayor Albino Balo, five former and current municipal officials and a private contractor for graft, following…

blocks.text: November 26, 2026 | 12:10pm
Philstar.com / File

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Ombudsman has affirmed its indictment of former Guindulman, Bohol Mayor Albino Balo, five former and current municipal officials and a private contractor for graft, following allegations that a giant Christmas tree was unlawfully passed off as a newly procured, government-funded billboard.

In separate orders issued on November 25, the Ombudsman also upheld the administrative dismissal from service of Balo and the five local government employees, affirming its earlier finding of Grave Misconduct.
The administrative ruling affirms a 2025 Ombudsman decision imposing dismissal from service on Balo, Labang, Janiola, Beronio, Hinatuan and Besinga.
With the criminal appeals exhausted at the Ombudsman level, formal Informations will now be filed against the six officials and Bernaldez before the appropriate court.
The investigation was triggered by a complaint filed by Bernard Banal regarding irregularities in Guindulman's 2023 Multi-Purpose Billboard Cell construction project.

According to the Ombudsman's findings, a giant Christmas tree erected in November 2022 was subsequently presented and billed to the municipal government as a newly constructed multi-purpose billboard in May 2023.

Investigators flagged the involvement of the municipal officials in processing, inspecting, and signing off on key transaction records, including the Inspection and Acceptance Report, Certificate of Acceptance and payment certifications, to facilitate the project.
In their appeals, Balo and his co-respondents contended that the project followed legitimate procurement protocols and maintained that they had acted in good faith.
The Ombudsman, however, dismissed their arguments, along with a separate appeal lodged by Bernaldez, ruling that there was no sufficient basis to overturn the initial finding of probable cause.

The anti-graft body maintained that the seven respondents violated Section 3(e) of Republic Act No. 3019, or the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act, citing evidence of alleged bad faith, manifest partiality, or gross inexcusable negligence.

In denying the motions for reconsideration filed by the respondents in the criminal probe, the Ombudsman stated that it found "no compelling reason to reverse, alter or modify its assailed Consolidated Resolution."
Alongside Balo, the municipal officials facing criminal indictment and dismissal are the following:

items: Rodney Jones Labang, Municipal Engineer
Jean Janiola, Municipal Treasurer
Ariston Beronio, Municipal Engineer
Evelyn Hinatuan, Administrative Aide III
Dennis Theodore Besinga, Administrative Aide II

blocks.text: Private contractor Emilio Bernaldez will also be charged with graft for his alleged role in the transaction.

articles.title: [Rear View] Sara Duterte’s farewell walk?
articles.summary: This is not a declared presidential candidate showing off the breadth of her political coalition. This is more like one thanking the people who stood by her as she prepares her exit.

blocks.text: Is it just me or is Vice President Sara Duterte doing the political version of a farewell walk?

Pageant bekis know the ritual, the one where the reigning queen, before relinquishing her crown, takes a long, almost leisurely walk on the runway, all smiles, waving at the adoring crowd while sentimental music plays in the background.

A pre-recorded speech plays alongside, where she takes stock of her reign, of her experiences and lessons learned, and ends with grateful thank yous to the organization and her fans. The camera follows her as she fades into the background. Behind the curtains, she no longer holds the spotlight, and she knows it.
Watch the Vice President these past days and you will see that walk.

A round of visits to Duterte strongholds, a profuse thanks to supporters for keeping her strong despite adversities, a year-end thanksgiving brunch with political personalities known for loyalty, but no heavyweights who signal leverage and clout.
This is not a declared presidential candidate showing off the breadth of her political coalition. This is more like one thanking the people who stood by her as she prepares her exit.
The whisper in political circles is that the 14 votes needed to convict are there.

Until the votes are in, it remains a whisper, and who knows, the Vice President might pull off a surprise in the Q&A or the Marcos administration’s operators might trip at the runway. But the Duterte camp surely has heard the whisper, and its behavior says it believes the whisper.

The impeachment trial resumes on Tuesday, December 1, and if the schedule holds, the verdict could come before Congress adjourns for Christmas. The verdict will surely be the topic at every family reunion and Noche Buena, along with grumblings over how this administration has made this Christmas season the most miserable since the pandemic lockdown.

Her critics, of course, do not expect her to walk off a winner. The Vice President has long proven she is no Miss Congeniality and after November, certainly not Best in National Costume either. Her defense spent the month showing us how ill-fitting the costume of a public servant living a simple lifestyle is.

The impeachment trial rests on a single article of unexplained wealth. The defense expressed confidence it could make a rebuttal on the prosecution’s forensic report showing alleged unexplained wealth and undeclared assets at P817.87 million. So far, it has failed to make a convincing one.

After announcing, then dropping, 16 bank officials from the list of witnesses, a move that, had it proceeded, would have provided an opening to question her joint account with her father, detained former President Rodrigo Duterte, the defense brought in their anti-money-laundering expert. But the said expert attacked the methodology of a forensic report he admitted he had not read. He also conceded the other claims he made in open court were outside his expertise.

A witness testifying on the banana chip company tied to the Vice President’s husband admitted that the company lacks the property, plant, equipment, and personnel needed to run a manufacturing business. Other witnesses tested the patience of senator-judges with their selective amnesia. Their testimonies only raised more questions and bolstered the case against the Vice President.
And through all of this, the Vice President herself has not taken the stand. The public, says a recent survey, now wants to hear her testify.

In 2012, then-chief justice Renato Corona took the stand at his impeachment trial. He was convicted anyway, but he showed up for his own Q&A. Sara Duterte has chosen to let her lawyers do the talking for her. That’s no way to keep the crown.

When the senator-judges hand in their scorecards, and if the whisper turn out to be true, it would be difficult, if not impossible, for the Vice President to wave and smile, or deliver a generous and sincere thank you for the memories. – Rappler.com
Joey Salgado is a former journalist, and a government and political communications practitioner. He served as spokesperson for former vice president Jejomar Binay.

articles.title: Trump tariff threat ‘unacceptable’, says Brazil, as China denounces levies as baseless
articles.summary: Brazil indignant about proposed tariffs on sugar and aircraft, while Beijing says new levies amount to ‘political manipulation’

blocks.text: Brazil has said it will not bend to the new US tariff “threat” and China accused Washington of “political manipulation” in the wake of Donald Trump’s latest economic salvo against 14 major trading partners.

Brazil’s government said on Wednesday: “Brazil will not yield to this type of threat”, adding in its statement that the “unilateral decision constitutes an unacceptable action within the framework of the ongoing bilateral negotiating process”.
It voiced particular indignation at US proposals for higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, a change that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker.

It added that Brazil would continue to negotiate “without ruling out the possibility of adopting retaliatory measures in response to the illegal and unjust imposition of tariffs on Brazilian products”.

Brazil was particularly singled out for in the announcement after trade talks stalled. The Trump administration claimed on Wednesday that the new tariffs would be consistent with trade deals that the US reached last year with dozens of countries.

The new tariffs are being imposed under a law which allowed the president to target countries the US had found to engage in unreasonable or discriminatory trade practices. Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative, told CNBC that many US trading partners had adopted “market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America’s manufacturing base.”
The administration will seek feedback from affected industries and hold a hearing on 25 January, suggesting the final duties won’t take effect until February or March.

China is potentially facing one of the biggest hits. The US said China would face the highest capped rate of 20%, which in some cases will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%. The US and China last year reached a trade truce but that is set to expire on 10 January 2027.
A spokesperson for China’s embassy in Washington rejected allegations that China was ‌a source of ⁠excess capacity, but stopped short of threatening retaliation.

“The so-called issue of ‘industrial overcapacity’ does not really exist and should not be used as a pretext for political manipulation,” the spokesperson said, urging the two sides to jointly deliver on agreements secured between Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

Earlier, China’s foreign ministry restated its opposition while calling for the US to resolve the issue through dialogue. “A tariff war or a trade war serves no party’s interests,” spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.

Greer told CNBC that the administration is proposing a “broad exemption” for $30bn worth of Chinese goods in line with the deal. “We’ve talked to our trading partners about this – they know what we’re proposing,” Greer told CNBC. “I think a lot of this is baked in.”
Some US analysts criticised the duties as too weak to change China’s trade practices.

China “is a bigger source of excess production than the rest of the world combined,” said Derek Scissors, senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. Yet Wednesday’s proposal “barely raises existing tariffs on China and will make no difference to the country’s trade behaviour.”
Vietnam’s trade ministry said it was ⁠working with the US to complete its trade deal as soon ⁠as possible and would coordinate with relevant US agencies.
It added it was “preparing ​and submitting ​rebuttal comments on the ​preliminary findings as well as on inaccurate submissions ​and allegations ‌made by ​interested ​parties.”

In response to the US announcement, the Indian government denied it had any structural excess capacity in ⁠any sector, ⁠adding that it remained committed to an early conclusion of ⁠a trade deal between the two countries. Greer has said the tariff ⁠on Indian imports would be capped at 17% if a trade deal was struck.
Taiwan was also singled out for new tariffs, but Taipei on Thursday said it was confident it would keep its existing ⁠15% tariff rate.

Taipei and Washington signed trade deals in January and February of ‌this year, which secured preferential treatment for semiconductors and other tech product which account for ​over 70% of Taiwan’s exports to the US.
Other countries and regions affected by the new tariffs include Bangladesh, ‌Cambodia, the European Union, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, and Thailand.
Tokyo’s top government spokesman, Minoru Kihara, said it was “regrettable that a proposed measure targeting Japan has been announced”.

Trump’s latest round of tariffs may be here to stay despite the Democrats’ electoral sweep in the US midterms. Some Democrats will likely support some of the tariffs, particularly on China. And Trump can veto any legislation that seeks to overturn the import taxes.
However Democratic Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, who will take over the finance committee next year, said he would “use every tool at my disposal to end Trump’s tariffs chaos.”

“This is another blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs,” Wyden added. “Global overcapacity is a serious problem, but Trump’s unilateral price-hiking tariffs are not the solution.”
With Associated Press and Reuters

articles.summary: Sen. JV Ejercito on Thursday, November 26, explained the rationale behind cutting social welfare allocations to give the Philippine Health Insurance Corp.’s budget a P19.8-billion increase to…

blocks.text: November 26, 2026 | 11:37am
In this undated photo shows people transacting at a Philippine Health Insurance Corp. office.
Philstar.com / Irra Lising

MANILA, Philippines — Sen. JV Ejercito on Thursday, November 26, explained the rationale behind cutting social welfare allocations to give the Philippine Health Insurance Corp.’s budget a P19.8-billion increase to support the implementation of the Universal Health Care Act.
In an interview with DZBB, Ejercito said that his P100-billion target for PhilHealth’s budget may not be reached due to shrinking fiscal space and declining government revenue.
The proposed realignment, however, represents a welcome increase, raising the insurance program’s budget to P94.2 billion from P73 billion.

The funds would come from cuts to the Department of Social Welfare and Development’s Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations program and the Medical Assistance Program, with each allocation reduced by P9.9 billion.
According to Ejercito, a larger PhilHealth budget would help expand the insurance program’s coverage and benefits, which can reinforce the Universal Health Care Act.
Under the Universal Health Care Act, every Filipino is automatically enrolled as a member of PhilHealth.
Those able to pay premiums are included as direct contributors. Certain groups, meanwhile, qualify as indirect contributors whose premiums are subsidized by the government.
PhilHealth’s budget funds programs like zero-balance billing, preventive care, immunization and health promotion, as well as enhancements to provincial and local health facilities.

Asked if infrastructure funds could cover the P6 billion needed to meet his budget target, Ejercito said these would remain allocated for their intended purpose, as his priority was to restore funding for foreign-assisted projects.
The allocations for these projects, which include railways and other public infrastructure, saw a P130-billion cut in the House of Representatives’ version of the budget.

This realignment in the House's version, which coincided with an increase in allocations for flood control projects and multi-purpose buildings, prompted intensified scrutiny of the budget at the Senate level.

articles.title: Australia projected to completely miss 2035 emissions target without new climate policies
articles.summary: New official projections show country nearly on track for 2030 goal but Chris Bowen warns of ‘undeniable headwinds’

blocks.text: Australia is nearly on track to reach its 2030 emissions reduction target but will fall massively short of a 2035 target unless the federal government substantially ramps up its climate policies, according to new official projections.

Under existing policies, the country is on track by 2035 to cut climate pollution by only 48% compared with 2005 levels – far below its target reduction of between 62% and 70% by that date, climate department projections suggest.
Australia’s progress towards the 2035 target has not improved since the last projection released a year ago.

In an annual climate statement to parliament on Thursday, the climate change and energy minister, Chris Bowen, said that while the country was “making good progress, we are facing undeniable headwinds”.

Bowen, speaking after a bruising experience over failed climate talks at Cop31, attacked the Queensland Liberal National government’s decision to “abandon its renewable energy targets and extend the operation of coal-fired power plants”, saying it would “significantly impact” national emissions.

“Continuing to sweat intermittent and unreliable coal just isn’t the answer to the question of our future energy security. And walking back previously approved renewable projects creates uncertainty, which then goes on to jeopardise future renewable investments,” he said. “Our system needs certainty. It does not need sovereign risk.”
The projections suggested Australia’s climate pollution was on track to be 42% below 2005 levels by 2030 – “within reach” of its 43% 2030 emissions reduction target.

However, that forecast assumes the government will reach its goal of 82% of electricity coming from renewable energy nationally by 2030. Several experts say that is unlikely to happen due to delays in the rollout of large-scale wind and farms and new transmission lines.
The department’s assessment said if unforeseen delays and supply chain bottlenecks pushed the 82% target back to 2032, Australia would only cut emissions by only 38% by 2030.

A separate report released on Thursday found that climate pollution fell by 1.3% – 6.2m tonnes – in the year to June. Bowen said this represented “a reduction at one-and-a-half times the rate of the last 10 years”. Australia’s total annual emissions were 25.3% below 2005 levels.

Emissions from generating electricity were down 3.6%, reflecting “record renewables generation and the ongoing displacement of coal and gas”. Gas generation fell by 23.2% and coal generation decreased by 3.6% over the year.

A third report, an annual progress assessment by another government agency, the Climate Change Authority, warned the country’s pace of emissions reduction must “accelerate substantially”. It said achieving the 2030 and 2035 targets would require sustained average annual emissions reductions of about 25m to 30m tonnes.

The authority found transport was approaching a “tipping point”, with electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles accounting for 29% of new light vehicle sales in 2026, up from 13% in 2025. The authority said more responsibility for emissions cuts would shift towards other areas, including “industry, resources, agriculture and other harder-to-abate activities”.

It warned additional action was needed to deal with methane – a potent greenhouse that amplifies global heating over a short time period. It recommended more be done to deploy established technologies, such as detecting and repairing leaks at mining sites and minimising avoidable venting and flaring of fossil fuel gas.

In a reply to Bowen’s climate statement, the shadow energy and emissions reduction minister, Dan Tehan, focused on electricity prices and the Cop31 breakdown – and the cost of free coffee at the Australian pavilion at the summit – rather than addressing the climate crisis.
He said national emissions had increased since Labor was elected in 2022, but did not mention that climate pollution was suppressed in 2022 due to economic shutdowns during the Covid-19 pandemic.
The Greens’ deputy leader and climate spokesperson, Steph Hodgins-May, said the government’s rhetoric on climate change “is just so far apart from the action”.
She said the government was basing its climate strategy on further electrification, “while still waving through new coal and gas”.
“They’re telling us they want to take climate action, but [are] simultaneously approving 38 new coal and gas mines,” Hodgins-May said.
The Australian Conservation Foundation’s head of advocacy, Gavan McFadzean, said the government report card showed strong progress in some areas but there was clear room for improvement.
“The renewables build is progressing, but it faces headwinds from uncooperative states and other forces whipping up opposition to wind and solar in rural communities for political purposes,” he said.
McFadzean said Australia’s exported emissions from the burning of coal and gas overseas, totalling 1.1 bn tonnes in 2025-26, “is not in this statement and remains a blind spot”.
“Exported emissions are the biggest handbrake on Australian climate action,” he said. “For Australia to be a positive climate player, we need to phase out exports of coal and gas.”

articles.title: As foreign troops withdraw from Somalia, could al-Shabab take over?
articles.summary: Somalia relies heavily on foreign funding and military support for its very survival.

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Some analysts fear Somali security forces may not be able to handle the nation's security without external support

Somalia is facing a fresh test of its stability as foreign troops begin withdrawing, funding for its security forces comes under pressure and a bitter political dispute threatens to derail plans for the country's first direct democratic elections in decades.
The combination of challenges has raised questions about whether the government can defend itself against Islamist militant group al-Shabab while managing growing divisions among political factions.
Some analysts fear the situation could embolden al-Shabab, which is affiliated with al-Qaeda, and potentially allow it to seize control of the capital, Mogadishu.
The group already controls large parts of the country despite the presence of about 12,000 African Union (AU) troops supporting the government.
The withdrawal of foreign forces, alongside the activities of clan-based militias aligned with rival political factions, has heightened concerns about the government's ability to maintain control.
Ugandan troops, who make up the largest contingent of the AU force, began withdrawing last month, with the country expected to complete its withdrawal by next year.

Ethiopia, another major contributor to the AU mission, is also reportedly planning to withdraw about 3,000 troops. The country has 2,500 troops authorised under the AU mission and roughly 5,000 under a bilateral agreement with Somalia. It is not clear whether the reported withdrawals would be from the AU contingent, the bilateral force, or both.

The US, which had earlier announced cuts to funding for the UN Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS) has since said it is extending it for a year. Washington contributes about a quarter of $500m UNSOS's annual budget, which supports Somali security forces, AU missions and individual troop-contributing nations.
With military support uncertain and the government facing mounting political challenges, analysts question whether Somalia's security forces are ready to stand on their own.

The concerns were heightened recently when al-Shabab claimed to have killed hundreds of elite Somali soldiers in an attack. The government acknowledged the attack but did not disclose the number of casualties.
Abdisalam Guleid, a former deputy director of Somalia's National Security Agency, told the BBC the security situation was increasingly precarious.
He warned that the withdrawal of foreign troops could leave Mogadishu vulnerable to a takeover similar to that of Afghanistan by the Taliban in 2021, following the withdrawal of US and Nato forces.
"I don't think Mogadishu will be able to defend itself. The Taliban style [takeover]… that's the most likely scenario I can envision now," he said.
The Taliban took over control of Afghanistan between 6-15 August 2021 in a rapid offensive, following the withdrawal of US and NATO forces.
Such a scenario has played out in Somalia in the past, Guleid explains.
Somalia has experienced the collapse of central authority before.
In the early 1990s, clan-based rebel groups advanced on Mogadishu from several fronts, forcing then-President Mohamed Siad Barre from power.

His overthrow triggered a devastating civil war and a prolonged humanitarian crisis. The collapse of state institutions subsequently created conditions in which Islamist militant groups, including al-Shabab, were able to expand their influence.
Guleid says Ugandan troops have been central to preventing a similar collapse since their first deployment to Somalia in 2007.

They played a key role in driving al-Shabab out of Mogadishu and other major towns, while protecting strategic installations, including the airport, seaport, government institutions and diplomatic missions.

Troops from Burundi, Djibouti, Kenya, Sierra Leone and Ethiopia later joined the AU mission, while countries including Turkey and the US maintained separate military deployments and provided training and equipment to Somali forces.
But Guleid argues that years of international assistance have not translated into sufficient military independence for the Somali government.
He says the authorities have become so reliant on foreign protection that they have neglected to adequately prepare their own forces to take over.
Somalia's Information Minister Abdifatah Qasim Mohamud rejected suggestions that the country would be unable to cope with the withdrawals.
He told the BBC that Somali troops had already taken over some positions vacated by Ugandan forces and were prepared to assume greater responsibility for the country's security.
He said Somalia could not depend indefinitely on foreign troops for its protection.
"I believe there is no reason for concern over this issue. There will be no change in the country's security situation or in the areas they have vacated," he said.
President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud has also been seeking continued international backing.
During a visit to Uganda on 23 November, he and President Yoweri Museveni called on the international community to continue supporting Somalia to consolidate security gains.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Uganda troops were first deployed to Somalia in 2007

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Uganda troops were first deployed to Somalia in 2007
Not everyone believes the withdrawal will necessarily result in a security collapse.
Ugandan security analyst Freddie David Egesa argues that years of international military support have helped Somalia establish the institutions needed to take greater responsibility for its security.
He says the withdrawal will provide an opportunity to assess how much progress has been made.
It will also force Somalia's political leaders to put aside their differences and take greater responsibility for the country's future, he adds.
But other analysts warn that the timing could hardly be worse.

Omar Mahmood, an analyst at the International Crisis Group, says Somali forces are under considerable pressure as they fight al-Shabab while attempting to take over positions previously held by foreign troops.
This is a major undertaking for an army that is still developing, he says.
The military is also facing pressure in the Bay region of the South-West state, where forces loyal to ousted regional President Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed have been fighting the federal government.
The withdrawal of Ugandan troops from the Lower Shabelle region could create further security challenges, Mahmood adds.
Mahmood further points to the long-delayed elections, which need to be secured, as another issue compounding the security situation.
Somalia has been attempting to move away from an indirect electoral system in which clan elders select lawmakers, who then elect the president, towards a system of direct voting.
Beyond the military situation, Mahmood says, the government must also resolve a growing political dispute over the timing and format of the country's elections.
But the proposed changes have divided the government and opposition, with disagreements over how the elections should be conducted.
The dispute escalated this year after Mohamud pushed through constitutional amendments extending the presidential term from four to five years, effectively delaying the next elections until 2027.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Al-Shabab militants still pose a big threat against the government

blocks.text: Al-Shabab militants still pose a big threat against the government
This month, the Supreme Court ruled against the extension, ordering political leaders to agree on an electoral roadmap within 30 days and to hold elections within three months.

A day before the ruling, Mohamud dismissed Chief Justice Baashe Yusuf Ahmed. He and other judges in the case have filed a suit against Somalia over the dismissals at the East African regional court in Tanzania.
The Somali government has since rejected the Supreme Court's decision, with its implementation now uncertain.
Mahmood says the political and security crises are closely connected, with the absence of consensus over the elections making it harder for the government to focus on the fight against al-Shabab.
Guleid also warns that the threat to Somalia's stability comes not only from the militant group but from clan-based militias increasingly challenging the federal government.
"Today, we have clan loyalists fighting alongside al-Shabab against the federal government," he said.
He added the country's leadership appears unable to anticipate the scale of the challenges ahead.
Who will fill the gap left by foreign partners?
Somalia's security challenges are compounded by its heavy dependence on international financial support.
Latest data from its finance ministry shows that donor grants amounting to $878.8m accounts for two-thirds of its planned $1.36bn budget in 2026.
Despite that, the ministry said it had only received about $314m of grants in the first nine months of the year, equivalent to 35% the expected annual aid.
Mahmood believes that although some international military support is declining, other partners could help bridge the gap through bilateral agreements and continued assistance.
But Guleid is sceptical that countries such as Turkey, Qatar and Egypt could quickly replace the military and financial contributions of Uganda and the US.
He argues that Somalia's dependence on external support makes it particularly vulnerable when international partners change their priorities.
That dependence has also contributed to increasingly strained relations with some foreign governments.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Somalia's challenges are compounded by its heavy reliance on foreign support

blocks.text: Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images
Somalia's challenges are compounded by its heavy reliance on foreign support

Somalia has accused the United Arab Emirates of funding armed groups and undermining its sovereignty, in the latest dispute involving an external power with significant security and economic interests in the country.
The UAE has rejected the criticism and hit back at the Somali leader, describing him as an "outgoing president" in reference to the dispute over his presidential mandate.
The two countries formally severed ties earlier this year, although the UAE has long been an important security and economic partner in Somalia.
The dispute illustrates the difficult relationship Somalia has with foreign partners on whom it relies for security, funding and political support.
For Egesa, the withdrawal of foreign troops could ultimately provide an opportunity for Somalia to demonstrate how much progress it has made in rebuilding its security institutions.
He believes the staggered departure of troops will allow Somali forces to assume responsibility gradually, while also forcing rival political factions to work together.
But Guleid remains far less optimistic.
He argues that unless Somalia addresses its military weaknesses, political divisions and growing influence of armed groups, it risks losing the security gains made.

For now, it faces the difficult task of fighting an entrenched insurgency, managing rival political interests and preparing for a contentious electoral process, all while some of military partners are preparing to leave.
Whether Somalia can withstand these pressures without renewed instability remains an open question.

articles.title: Sandiganbayan suspends Pasay judge over bribery case
articles.summary: The judge contests the suspension, claiming only the Supreme Court has the authority to discipline judges, but the Sandiganbayan maintains that its criminal proceedings are separate from…

blocks.text: The judge contests the suspension, claiming only the Supreme Court has the authority to discipline judges, but the Sandiganbayan maintains that its criminal proceedings are separate from administrative actions taken by the SC

items: The Sandiganbayan has ordered a three-month preventive suspension for Pasay City Judge Albert Cansino due to a direct bribery charge filed by the Office of the Ombudsman.
Cansino and court interpreter Mariejoy Lagman are accused of soliciting and receiving P6 million for a favorable decision in a property dispute, following an entrapment operation by the NBI.

Cansino contested the suspension, claiming only the Supreme Court could discipline judges, but the Sandiganbayan upheld the suspension, stating that administrative and criminal proceedings are distinct.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The anti-graft court Sandiganbayan has ordered the three-month preventive suspension of a Pasay City regional judge who is facing a direct bribery charge filed in August by the Office of the Ombudsman.

The Sandiganbayan’s 6th Division rejected Pasay Regional Trial Court Branch 108 Judge Albert Cansino’s opposition, citing Section 13 of the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act, which makes preventive suspension mandatory for public officials facing a valid charge under the law involving fraud against the government or public funds or property.
Cansino was charged together with court interpreter Mariejoy Lagman over the alleged solicitation and receipt, directly or indirectly, of P6 million from a litigant in a property dispute.

blocks.caption: Ombudsman Remulla: Corruption in judiciary also ‘severe’

blocks.text: The order was signed by associate justices Sarah Jane Fernandez, Kevin Narce Vivero and Lord Villanueva, and directed the Office of the Court Administrator to enforce the suspension.

The bribery case stemmed from the May 23, 2024 arrest of Lagman in an entrapment operation conducted by the National Bureau of Investigation. The operation followed an anonymous complaint sent to the Judicial Integrity Board.

NBI agents found during the arrest a copy of a May 15, 2024 order signed by Cansino. A certified true copy of the order had been received by a representative of the defendants in the Pasay court property dispute.
The P6 million was allegedly sought as a “consideration for a favorable decision” in the civil case.
Cansino argued against the Sandiganbayan’s authority to suspend him, arguing that only the Supreme Court had the power to discipline and suspend judges.
He said the SC had already placed him under preventive suspension for 90 days in 2024 over the same allegations, extending the measure twice for a total of nine months.
Cansino said he resumed his judicial duties in February 2025 “without issue, interference, or untoward incident.”
But the Sandiganbayan rejected the argument, saying the SC’s suspension was imposed in an administrative proceeding, while the case before it was criminal in nature.

“This Court must, however, emphasize that administrative proceedings are separate and distinct from criminal proceedings, even if the said proceedings arose from the same facts and circumstances,” the anti-graft court said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: U.S. judge blocks FCC from revoking licences of Disney-owned ABC stations
articles.summary: A U.S. ‌judge on Wednesday barred the Federal Communications Commission from revoking Walt Disney's licences for its eight company-owned ABC TV stations, in a dramatic blow to President Donald…

image.caption: U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) chair Brendan Carr speaking during a press conference in Washington in July. A judge said Carr 'has taken President Trump's rhetoric as his marching orders' in a decision Wednesday that blocked the FCC from revoking the licences of eight ABC TV stations.

blocks.text: World·New

A U.S. ‌judge on Wednesday barred the Federal Communications Commission from revoking Walt Disney's licences for its eight company-owned ABC TV stations, in a dramatic blow to President Donald Trump's efforts to rein in American media companies.
Ruling is a blow to Trump's efforts to rein in American media firms

"This is not a close case," US District Judge Loren Alikhan wrote. ABC has a "weighty interest in 'vindicating ​their right to be free of retaliation for [their] protected speech,'" the judge wrote ​in a case that was a key test of the free-speech rights of media outlets.
The judge said the FCC appears to be carrying out a retaliatory campaign driven by Trump.
FCC chair ​Brendan Carr, who was tapped to lead the agency in January 2025, "has taken President Trump's ⁠rhetoric as his marching orders," the ⁠judge added.

Trump has repeatedly urged broadcasters to drop ‌comedy or news programs that he dislikes or that have been critical of him or his administration. He has also pressed the FCC on a number of occasions to revoke ABC's licences.
Carr, the White House, Disney and ABC did not immediately respond to requests for comment late on Wednesday.
Reviews ordered in April

Disney and ABC sued ⁠the FCC in August to block an unprecedented early review of licences for eight ABC stations, arguing that the Trump administration was trying to punish the network over its broadcast content.

Carr ordered the reviews in April, even though the stations' licence renewals ‌were not scheduled to be considered before October 2028. The FCC had not ordered an early review in more than 50 years before April.

items: ABC sues U.S. broadcast regulator over early licence reviews, calling it an 'existential threat'
Trump says ABC should fire Jimmy Kimmel over his 'expectant widow' joke

blocks.text: The reviews were ordered in April, a day after Trump urged ABC to fire late-night host Jimmy Kimmel.

Broadcast stations need FCC licences to use public airwaves. While licence revocations ​are extremely rare, critics say the threat of losing a licence can pressure broadcasters and raise concerns about government interference in editorial and programming decisions. Networks have broad ⁠free-speech protections over programming choices.
Jimmy Kimmel’s Melania 'widow' joke | About That

Trump has waged an aggressive series of attacks on the news media and the latest move ⁠follows a two-year-long battle between Trump and Disney. In July, Trump again called for ABC stations to lose their ⁠licences ⁠because the network refused to air a prime-time ​speech on elections.

The FCC is also investigating ABC daytime talk show The View, which discusses U.S. politics, after saying it may ​be subject to federal rules requiring ⁠broadcasters to provide equal-time opportunities to political candidates.
Disney noted earlier that as a result, the program did not invite any political candidates to appear ahead of the November midterm elections, citing the FCC's "pressure campaign."

Trump has also been more broadly criticized by free-speech advocates for attempting to target critics, deport foreign student protesters and freeze federal funds for educational institutions. His efforts have faced legal challenges ⁠and some judicial setbacks.
