articles.title: California warned of potential Thanksgiving flooding as storms threaten US coasts
articles.summary: Parts of the Canadian province of British Columbia may also be affected by the storms, which come as millions of people travel for the holiday.

blocks.text: Coastal areas of California are bracing for potential flooding as king tides peak in the state during the US Thanksgiving holiday.

Water levels across the US state's vast coastline could reach over 8ft (2.4 metres) in some areas on Wednesday and Thursday, according to the National Weather Service (NWS) - breaking records set just last month.
The NWS has warned parts of California could face major coastal flooding, which is likely to be significant in low-lying areas. There have already been some reports of flooding.
Meanwhile, storms are also forecast for the Pacific Northwest, including the Canadian province of British Columbia, and eastern parts of the US.
Portions of a pier in northern California came crashing down into the ocean on Wednesday as high tides and strong waves battered the structure, video showed.
Beachgoers have been advised to stay away from the water's edge as large waves could suddenly form. Such waves could be damaging to piers and jetties, and could capsize small vessels, the NWS warned.
Flooding has already been reported in the San Francisco Bay Area.

In San Diego, a high tide of 8 ft 11in was recorded on Wednesday morning local time - potentially breaking the record for highest tide measured in the area, which was just set late last month at 7.98ft.
In Los Angeles, the tide on Wednesday was thought to be as high 8.19 - the record for the city that was set only weeks ago 27 October when parts of the California coast experienced flooding.
Recently set high tide records were also broken in Santa Barbara and La Jolla, according to preliminary data.
King tides are the highest predicted tide of the year and are above the highest water level reached at high tide on an average day.

While they typically occur once or twice a year in most coastal areas, they are happening more frequently in some as sea levels rise. These king tides are being strengthened by the strongest El Niño weather pattern on record.

Storm systems are also expected to impact the US through the Thanksgiving holiday - one affecting the Pacific Northwest and another the eastern part of the country, the US National Weather Service said.
On the east coast, a developing Nor'easter storm is expected to bring heavy rain, strong winds, and coastal flooding.
Major impacts are expected to begin on Wednesday across the southeast, and move northward Wednesday night and on Thursday, the NWS said.
"Those along the eastern seaboard can expect gusty, possibly damaging winds, heavy rain, and major coastal and marine impacts," it added.
The developing storm system could bring about one to four inches rain along America's east coast and a peak of four to six inches in coastal North Carolina.

The US department store chain Macy's has postponed its 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York, which was due to take place on Thursday, until Saturday because of severe weather - the first time this has happened.
The stormy weather on both coasts could disrupt travel for millions of people.
The American Automobile Association (AAA) has predicted that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles (80km) from home for Thanksgiving between Tuesday 24 November and Monday 30 November.
Officials have also issued a flood warning along Vancouver's coastline in Canada's most western province of British Columbia.
Residents were urged to take "immediate action to protect life and property", a weather warning from Environment and Climate Change Canada said.
King tides were expected to potentially increase already high water levels there too.

articles.title: How China got access to Nvidia’s AI chips despite rules to stop them
articles.summary: The drama around Nvidia, the top US exporter of AI chips to China, thrusts the rules into the spotlight

blocks.text: NVIDIA AND CHINA. The Nvidia logo and Chinese flag are seen in this illustration taken August 27, 2025.
Dado Ruvic/Reuters
The drama around Nvidia, the top US exporter of AI chips to China, thrusts the rules into the spotlight

items: AI chips are a key focus in the US-China technology competition, with the US implementing strict export controls to limit China's access to advanced semiconductor technology.
Recent regulations have complicated the export landscape, particularly affecting companies like Nvidia, which must navigate licensing requirements to ship AI chips to China.

The Trump administration's new rules aim to prevent chip smuggling to China by expanding licensing requirements to Southeast Asian countries, while ongoing investigations raise concerns about illegal diversion of US technology.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

AI chips are a central battleground in the US-China technology race. To preserve its lead, in recent years Washington has imposed and revised rules to restrict China’s access to advanced semiconductors and chipmaking technology, while balancing national security concerns with trade considerations.
The drama around Nvidia, the top US exporter of AI chips to China, has thrust those rules into the spotlight.
Delving into the resulting regulations is a quagmire. Export control rules are often likened to the US tax code in their complexity and constant revision.
Here are some basics for understanding what’s legal, and what’s not, when it comes to China’s access to US AI chips:
In October 2022, the US unveiled sweeping restrictions on advanced chips to China, marking the biggest shift in US policy toward exporting technology to China in decades.

A year later, it tightened the rules to capture more chips and stop chip designers such as Nvidia from selling products engineered to fall just below the performance thresholds of the earlier restrictions. It also expanded the restrictions to countries in the Middle East and restricted chips to overseas companies headquartered in China.

In January 2025, the Biden administration extended the restrictions globally, imposing a worldwide license requirement. But in May, days before it was set to take effect, the Trump administration announced it would not enforce that rule.

The Trump administration only formally rescinded and replaced the rule last week, leaving a gap that allowed data center capacity to proliferate in countries such as Singapore, where Chinese companies could rent computing power remotely to train and deploy AI models.
Did Megaspeed, the Singapore cloud company whose former executive allegedly had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, operate legally?

For over two years, authorities have been investigating whether Megaspeed diverted chips to China, which would be illegal. But companies in countries including Singapore were allowed to buy advanced AI chips for their data centers license-free until the US issued a new rule last week cutting off that practice.

Megaspeed likely won’t be getting any more chips. It was added to a US trade blacklist this week, along with its Thai and Malaysian subsidiaries, essentially blocking shipments. Nvidia also said it cut off sales to Megaspeed in June 2025.

About a year ago, President Donald Trump allowed Nvidia to ship its H200 chip to China, drawing criticism from experts who said the chips would help jumpstart China’s military modernization and erode the US lead in AI. The H200 chip is one of Nvidia’s more advanced chips, but not top-of-the-line.

Nvidia cannot simply ship the chips to Chinese companies that pay for them. Nvidia must apply for licenses from the US Department of Commerce, which has issued them since last spring on a case-by-case basis.

Last week, the House foreign affairs committee released licensing data showing the Trump administration approved shipments of nearly 900,000 advanced AI chips made by Nvidia and AMD for Chinese companies from December 2025 through May 2026.

Last week, the Trump administration issued a new regulation, adding license requirements for five countries including Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand, in an effort to crack down on chips being smuggled into China.

Prior to that, the chip-based license requirement generally applied to countries like Russia that raise national security concerns, along with companies headquartered in arms-embargoed countries. Now they also apply to Southeast Asian countries viewed as transshipment points with a high risk for illegal diversion to China.
The rule also clamped down on AI chip sales to non-US data centers that supply a high volume of computing power to Chinese-headquartered firms.
For years, Nvidia’s Huang has said there is no evidence of chip smuggling to China.

But that assertion, which experts already viewed skeptically, was further questioned in March when US prosecutors charged three people associated with California-based AI server maker Super Micro Computer SMCI.O, including its co-founder, in a scheme to divert about $2.5 billion of US technology into China, including AI servers packed with Nvidia AI chips.

Critics say Nvidia has tried to minimize a well-known risk. Huang once said Nvidia’s sophisticated Grace Blackwell AI chip platform weighed nearly 1.8 metric tons and could not fit into a pocket or backpack. But servers are not smuggled in backpacks. They are routed through third countries and intermediary companies.
Supporters say Nvidia may not have had verified evidence of diversion and that the company cannot keep tabs on all its products after they’re sold.

Nvidia has built location verification technology that could indicate which country its chips are operating in, the company confirmed in December 2025. It has offered the feature as a software option for customers.
But the company has opposed proposed legislation that would require location verification and diversion reporting for advanced AI processors.

A measure known as the Chip Security Act is among several export control bills that gained new momentum in the wake of the Nvidia scandal, and may be included in the National Defense Authorization Act that Congress is expected to pass next month. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Poilievre claims constituent's job was threatened after meeting at CFB Wainwright
articles.summary: Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says one of his constituents — a nurse who helped treat soldiers burned in the CFB Wainwright fire — is having her employment threatened because she met with him.

image.caption: This photo of nurse Maureen Carpenter was posted online by Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre on Oct. 20, 2026. (Pierre Poilievre/Facebook)

blocks.text: Politics·New
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says one of his constituents — a nurse who helped treat soldiers burned in the CFB Wainwright fire — is having her employment threatened because she met with him.
Nurse treating soldiers is being harassed, Opposition leader says in House of Commons
In an unusual speech in the House of Commons on Wednesday evening, Poilievre said his parliamentary privilege is being breached.

Last month, Maureen Carpenter was photographed speaking to Poilievre following the fire that killed five soldiers and wounded 38 others on Oct. 17. Poilievre said she is under contract with Calian Health, a government contractor, and works as a nurse.

"Maureen spoke to me on base, with the permission of the unit commander. I had the permission of the base commander to be there. She talked about caring for our men and women on the shift that night, that horrendous night," said Poilievre.

An online post from Oct. 20 shows Poilievre meeting with medical staff at CFB Wainwright Health Services. Online comments identify the woman in the photo as Carpenter, which was confirmed by Poilievre's office.
(Pierre Poilievre/Facebook)

"We owe Maureen as well as colleagues like her, our greatest gratitude. That is what I conveyed in our conversation. Instead, Maureen tells me that she's been threatened by Calian Health, all because she spoke to her local member of Parliament."
Poilievre is the MP for Wainwright, Alta., residents. The base is part of his federal riding of Battle River-Crowfoot.

He said, following the meeting, Carpenter was subject to a complaint and threatened — told by her boss that if her term contract was not already coming to an end, she would be put under the microscope by the company's legal department.
"The implicit message was that her contract would no longer have any chance of renewal, something that she had taken for granted before that point," Poilievre said.
Neither Calian nor Carpenter responded immediately to a request for comment.

Poilievre said Carpenter was told she violated the company's policy by meeting with her MP. He said there is no such policy — there is a rule against speaking to the media, but nothing prohibiting speaking to a member of Parliament.
'My intention was not for this to be politicized': Poilievre raises rare point of privilege

He said being able to speak to an MP is a right guaranteed under the Charter, and a requirement in order to ensure Canadians get good government. During the conversation, he said they discussed better support for mental health following the fires.
He said they did not discuss her company or workplace.
Poilievre said that when he heard from Carpenter, he raised the issue with the minister responsible. His office later confirmed he meant Defence Minister David McGuinty.
McGuinty's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
"My intention was not for this to be politicized. I simply wanted it to be solved," Poilievre said.
"Based on his original assurances, I had hoped the minister would put Calian in its place … but her family is indicating that the problems have worsened and there is no end in sight."
Poilievre moved a motion to refer the matter to the procedure and House affairs committee for investigation.

"Ideally though, the government and Calian will instead simply say sorry and fix the problem," he said. "But until and unless that happens, my ability to represent my constituents has been interfered with and you must denounce this conduct."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kate McKenna is a senior reporter with CBC’s parliamentary bureau in Ottawa, where she covers federal politics. She previously worked for CBC’s The Fifth Estate and in the Halifax, Montreal and Charlottetown newsrooms. Her investigative and breaking news coverage has won five RTDNA awards. She is the author of No Choice: The 30-Year Fight for Abortion on Prince Edward Island.

articles.title: 76% of Australians struggling to tell apart real and AI content – new report
articles.summary: The challenge is not just that AI-generated content is becoming more realistic. It’s that many people are unsure whether they’re able to recognize it at all.

blocks.text: AI. 'AI Artificial Intelligence' words, a keyboard and a robotics hand in this illustration taken, September 23, 2026
Dado Ruvic/Reuters
The challenge is not just that AI-generated content is becoming more realistic. It’s that many people are unsure whether they’re able to recognize it at all.

items: A significant majority of Australians (76%) have encountered AI-generated content they initially believed was real, highlighting challenges in distinguishing between AI and human-made content.

Despite high usage of AI tools, trust in them remains low, with only a minority expressing trust in major platforms like ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot, and a strong desire for safeguards and transparency in AI-generated content.

Education and AI literacy are crucial for improving recognition of synthetic content, with calls for a national approach to media and AI literacy education to better equip Australians in navigating the evolving digital landscape.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Most Australians are using – or at least have tried out – generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT, Copilot and Gemini, among many others.

We can use them to search for information, answer questions, and generate text, images, sound and video. As generative AI becomes more sophisticated and ubiquitous, many people are no longer able to distinguish AI-generated content from authentic, human-made content.

Our new representative survey of 2,000 Australian adults conducted in August and September 2026 found 76% of Australians had recently encountered content they initially believed was real, only to later discover that it had been generated by AI.

blocks.caption: Lessons for the Philippines: AI content surge bypassed Brazil’s election rules — report

blocks.text: People with high levels of education who are interested in the technology and have high AI literacy are the most likely to report having mistaken AI content for real.
However, this doesn’t mean these groups are more exposed or susceptible to AI-generated content. Instead, the data suggests these people are better at recognizing when they’ve been misled.
In fact, people with low education and lower AI literacy are the most likely to say they don’t know whether they have mistaken AI content for real.
Therefore, many Australians may not recognize when they have encountered synthetic content. This presents a dilemma for users who are increasingly turning to AI tools to seek information.

While AI use has grown rapidly, many are skeptical of the technology and concerned about how it might impact society. About half (51%) of Australian respondents said they use AI chatbots or tools at least weekly, and more than one quarter (28%) use them daily. Almost everyone (96%) is aware of at least one generative AI platform.

Despite widespread awareness and usage, trust in major AI tools remains very low. When asked “how much do you trust or distrust generative AI chatbots or tools?” only a minority said they trust ChatGPT (34%), Microsoft Copilot (24%), Google Gemini (24%) and Claude (17%).

Our survey also shows people are particularly distrustful of politicians and social media companies that use generative AI. More than half of Australians believe the use of AI by politicians and political parties will make society worse, with social media companies and news media viewed almost as negatively.

In contrast, the report reveals that people view scientists and healthcare professionals as the most trustworthy and benevolent users of AI, with around half saying their use of the technology will improve society.
Despite this high level of exposure to AI-generated content and low levels of trust, people rarely use proactive measures to identify or verify if content was AI-generated.

blocks.caption: Maria Ressa on AI overreliance: ‘Don’t outsource the nuances’

blocks.text: When people suspect AI-generated content, the majority simply take a closer look and examine the content carefully, relying on their intuition. Some check comments made by other online users. But few people look for disclosure statements or labels to identify whether it was made with AI, and even fewer turn to trusted sources of news.

Rather than engaging in lateral reading – leaving the content and checking independent sources – most people engage in vertical reading, which involves only looking within the source. They scrutinize the content itself and rely on their own judgment. This approach becomes less effective as AI-generated content becomes increasingly convincing.

Generally, younger people are more likely to check whether information is true, using a range of verification strategies. The exception is checking a trusted news source, which is more common among those aged 45 and over. Instead, young adults are far more likely to look at comments from other users than older age groups.

Additionally, AI literacy plays an important role in people’s verification strategies. Those with high AI literacy are much more likely to closely examine content than those with low understanding of the technology, suggesting that education about how AI works supports more active and critical evaluation of online information.
Because of the low levels of trust in the technology, Australians say they want strong safeguards around it.
Most importantly, they want protections to ensure accuracy and reliable responses when they are using an AI platform.

They also want guardrails in place to prevent AI from generating illegal, dangerous or harmful content, and protections to reduce the presence of bias and ensure fairness and equity in the content it generates.
This points to the need for a multi-pronged response from the tech platforms and government.

First, digital platforms need clearer and more consistent labeling of AI-generated content. If people are expected to make informed decisions about what they’re seeing, they need transparent information about where that content comes from.
Second, the findings show people with higher levels of AI literacy are better equipped to recognize synthetic content and engage in more critical evaluation practices.

We need to educate all Australians with media and AI literacy. Education in schools is important, but adults need training too. We need a whole-of-society approach where adults can have access to education through local community or workplace initiatives.

Australia already lags behind other countries when it comes to media literacy education, and the rapid increase in AI only makes the need for a national approach more urgent. – via Reuters/Rappler.com

articles.title: Family of homicide victim Trina Hunt files civil lawsuit against her husband
articles.summary: The lawsuit, filed by Trina's mother, brother and sister-in-law, asks the B.C. Supreme Court to declare that Iain Hunt killed his wife Trina, and make him hand over any property he inherited from her…

image.caption: The remains of Port Moody woman Trina Hunt, 48, were found near Hope, B.C., in March 2021. Now, her family is seeking to have a court declare that her husband Iain killed Trina, and make him hand over any property he inherited. (Twitter/Port Moody Police)

blocks.text: British Columbia·New

The lawsuit, filed by Trina's mother, brother and sister-in-law, asks the B.C. Supreme Court to declare that Iain Hunt killed his wife Trina, and make him hand over any property he inherited from her after her death.
Lawsuit asks court to declare that Iain Hunt killed his wife, make him hand over any property he inherited
A civil lawsuit has been filed against Iain Hunt, the husband of homicide victim Trina Hunt, who was charged with indignity to human remains in relation to her death.

The lawsuit, filed by Trina's mother, brother and sister-in-law, asks the B.C. Supreme Court to declare that Iain killed Trina, and make him hand over any property he inherited from her after her death.
Trina's remains were found near Hope, B.C., in March 2021 — two months after her husband reported her missing from her house in Port Moody.
Police charged him with indignity to human remains in relation to her death, which police have said is a homicide. However, no murder or manslaughter charges have been laid in the case.
Iain Hunt is seen in December 2018. He was charged in February 2025 with one count of indignity to human remains in relation to his wife's death. (Ben Nelms/CBC)
The civil lawsuit states that Iain intentionally misled Trina's family by reporting Trina missing, even though he knew where her body was.

"Mr. Hunt continued the charade by initially participating in a reward for information concerning Trina's disappearance and continuing to assert he knew nothing of her death when he knew all the time that Trina was dead, and he knew the location of her body," the lawsuit states.

items: Attorney general applies to stop disclosure in case against Iain Hunt, citing threat to national security
Court appearance delayed for husband of homicide victim Trina Hunt

blocks.text: The notice of civil claim said that the family relied on Iain's statements as being truthful, which led to concerted public efforts to find the Port Moody woman and raise awareness of her case.
Before Trina Hunt's remains were found, supporters organized extensive search efforts as well as online and in-person campaigns to raise awareness of her case.
Online court records show Iain allegedly interfered with his wife's remains on Jan. 16, 2021, two days before he reported her missing.
Family and supporters of Trina Hunt are seen outside a Port Coquitlam courthouse in March 2025, during an appearance by Iain Hunt. (Ben Nelms/CBC)
'Mental anguish and distress'

The lawsuit says that Iain's actions continue to cause the family "mental anguish and distress," and it seeks special damages for funeral costs and other costs, in addition to making the court hand over any property he inherited.

In the notice of civil claim, Trina's family claims Iain sold the property he co-owned with his wife in May 2023 for $1.92 million, and subsequently bought a property in the rural Fraser Valley community of Harrison Mills.
The family says that property was bought with the funds he obtained by selling the Port Moody house, which he bought with his wife in 2006 for just over $632,000.
Trina's family is seeking a certificate of pending litigation against the Harrison Mills property, as well as a tracing order for all the assets he inherited from Trina after her "wrongful death."

Frank Jang with the Integrated Homicide Investigation Team (IHIT) holds up a picture of Trina Hunt during a May 2021 news conference. Police have said Trina's death is a homicide, but no one has been charged with murder or manslaughter in relation to her death. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

A charge of indignity to human remains "occurs when a person neglects to perform their legal duty to bury a dead human body, or if a person interferes in an improper, indecent or undignified way with a dead human body or human remains," according to police.
None of the lawsuit's allegations have been proven in court.
Iain Hunt's next court appearance, in relation to the indignity to human remains charge, is in September 2027.

articles.title: [Vantage Point] The Marcos estate tax: A test of presidential statesmanship
articles.summary: Taking the high ground would give real substance to the President’s own appeals for tax compliance

blocks.text: Ferdinand Marcos Jr. can help settle his father’s estate tax and show Filipinos that the law applies with equal force when the taxpayer is the President’s own family.

When President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. opened the 2025 tax campaign of the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR), he asked Filipinos to pay what they owe. That call for civic duty gained urgency on November 13, when he swore in Rolando Ligon Jr. as BIR commissioner.

Ligon takes office facing a test that strikes at his bureau’s credibility: what has the government done to collect the unpaid estate tax of Ferdinand Marcos Sr.? While the duty to account and collect rests with the commissioner, the President can make that work far easier.

By publicly assuring the BIR that it has his full backing to pursue every lawful remedy—even when the taxpayer is his own family—Marcos Jr. can turn a decades-old stalemate into an act of true statesmanship.

Understanding what is at stake begins with the record. The starting figure is P23,293,607,638, per the assessment made by the BIR in July 1991 after a special audit found that no estate tax return had been filed.
PCGG, BIR Letters Re Marcos Estate Tax by Nami Buan on Scribd

Because Philippine jurisprudence, as affirmed in Lorenzo v. Posadas, establishes that succession taxes accrue at death, the original assessment is governed by the tax laws in force when the elder Marcos died in 1989.

The flat 6% estate tax rate introduced decades later under the TRAIN Law (Tax Reform for Acceleration and Inclusion Act or Republic Act No. 10963) does not apply to that assessment. (READ: [Ask the Tax Whiz] Estate tax amnesty: Essential compliance guide)
Instead, the tax code then in force imposed a graduated schedule peaking at 60% on any portion of a net estate exceeding P3 million, plus a P1,393,450 base tax on the first P3 million.

Working backward from the P23.29 billion assessment—subtracting the base tax, dividing the remainder by 60%, and adding back the initial P3 million—implies a taxable net estate of roughly P38.82 billion if the assessment consisted entirely of basic tax. (READ: Facts and lies: the Marcoses’ unpaid estate tax)

While that arithmetic illustrates the assessment’s scale, reconstructing the actual tax base requires the audit schedules showing which assets were included, how they were valued, and what deductions were allowed.

Public debate, however, has often centered on P203.819 billion. That figure stems from a 2021 calculation by retired Supreme Court senior associate justice Antonio Carpio, who took the P23.294 billion assessment and added a 25% surcharge of P5.823 billion, P139.762 billion in interest at 20% a year over 30 years, and P34.940 billion in interest on the surcharge. (READ: [ANALYSIS] The estate tax liability of the Marcos Estate)

The math explains how the headline number grew, yet its assumptions require an official accounting. The TRAIN Law changed how statutory interest is calculated starting January 1, 2018, and the Supreme Court has applied the transition from 20% to 12% in tax cases. The BIR should clarify which rates and periods govern this account, how each charge was computed, and what credits reduce the balance.

What is beyond dispute is that the assessment itself is legally settled. Marcos personally challenged the collection measures decades ago, leading to the Supreme Court’s 1997 ruling in Marcos II v. Court of Appeals.

The Court held that the assessment became final and unappealable after the heirs failed to protest it through proper channels, finding sufficient notice and timely levies under the three-year prescriptive period then applicable.

Crucially, the justices ruled that the BIR could proceed against estate property without waiting for probate court approval. Though Marcos claimed in 2022 that his family could not argue its case while in Hawaii, the Court’s decision records that notices were served after his return to the Philippines—including papers for his mother delivered through his office at the House of Representatives.
The coalition 1Sambayan is urging Ligon to act before December 2, marking five years since the BIR sent a written demand to the heirs—a notice confirmed by then-commissioner Caesar Dulay.

Determining whether another demand letter is legally necessary to preserve the government’s claims requires reviewing the statute and the collection record. As the Supreme Court showed in Republic v. Hizon—where a collection suit was deemed time-barred even as the BIR was allowed to proceed against properties covered by timely warrants—deadlines matter. Ligon must swiftly establish which remedies remain live and act accordingly before any applicable window closes. (READ: [Ask the Tax Whiz] The new BIR chief’s 3 crosses: Will he dare audit the powerful?)

Just as importantly, the BIR owes the public a transparent accounting of past collection steps. Court records show that 11 Tacloban, Leyte, parcels went to auction in 1993. When no one bid, the properties were declared forfeited to the government.

What became of those lands, and what value, if any, was credited against the tax? Subject to lawful disclosure limits, the bureau should lay out the full ledger: the original assessment, accrued charges, recoveries, and collectible balance. If any remedy has lapsed, it should explain when and why. After years of competing figures, Filipinos deserve a clear record they can examine.

This moment gives Marcos a rare chance to show statesmanship. As an heir, he can help produce estate records, authorize disclosures where his consent can lawfully enable them, and work with the other heirs to settle what the BIR confirms is due.

As President, he can give Ligon the space to reach and explain his own conclusions, even those inconvenient to the Marcos family. He can do both before December 2, while the bureau determines that date’s legal significance.

Taking the high ground would give real substance to the President’s own appeals for tax compliance and hand revenue officers a powerful precedent the next time a well-connected taxpayer expects special treatment.

Marcos has spent years asking Filipinos to judge his administration on its merits. Now, the choice is his. By using the authority of his office to protect the BIR’s independence in pursuing his father’s estate, he can show Filipinos that the law bends for no one. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Brad Pitt, Angelina Jolie settle dispute over French estate Château Miraval
articles.summary: Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie have reached a settlement in their contentious dispute over the French winery and estate Château Miraval, where they were wed.

image.caption: Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie have settled their contentious dispute over their French winery and estate. (Jordan Strauss/Invision/AP and Andrew Medichini/AP)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie have reached a settlement in their contentious dispute over the French winery and estate Château Miraval, where they were wed.
Allegations of abuse emerged in court filings during contentious legal battle
"We have settled out of court in the best interests of our family and will not be commenting further," Pitt and Jolie's representatives told CBC News in a joint statement on Wednesday afternoon.
"Any comments in media stories attributed to 'sources' are in fact not coming from either of us, or anyone close to us," they added.
Terms of the settlement were not disclosed.

The Hollywood couple, formerly dubbed Brangelina, had leased the 1,200-acre vineyard and estate — located in Correns, in the southern French region of Provence — back in 2008, eventually purchasing it.
The Château Miraval property in Correns, located in the southern French region of Provence, is seen in 2008. (Lionel Cironneau/Associated Press)
It was the site of the pair's wedding in 2014. At the time of their nuptials, the duo had been romantic partners for about a decade.
However, just two years later, Jolie filed for divorce, citing irreconcilable differences.

items: Vivienne Jolie drops dad Brad Pitt's last name, following 3 other siblings

blocks.text: Their split — which involved a bitter custody dispute and allegations of abuse levelled at Pitt — dragged out for eight years, with the A-list Hollywood actors ultimately reaching a divorce settlement in late December 2024.
Duelling lawsuits over estate

In fall 2021, Jolie sold her half of Château Miraval to a wine subsidiary of Russian businessman Yuri Shefler's SPI Group, the international consortium that sells Stoli vodka and other alcohol brands worldwide.
Pitt sued her and Shefler over the sale in 2022, contending that he and Jolie had previously agreed to seek each other's consent before selling their stakes.
Angelina Jolie, second from left, attends the premiere of her movie Maria with her children Pax, left, Zahara, second right, and Maddox in New York in 2024. (Evan Agostini/Invision/Associated Press)

Jolie countersued and — in a subsequent court filing tied to the winery dispute — made public for the first time a raft of details about the in-flight confrontation involving the pair and their children in 2016 that prompted her, days later, to file for divorce.

items: Angelina Jolie describes Brad Pitt's allegedly abusive behaviour in court filing

blocks.text: Jolie alleged in the filing that she and her children had experienced physical and verbal abuse from Pitt while on that private flight, en route from Château Miraval to their home in Los Angeles. The incident was investigated at the time, and no charges were filed against Pitt.
Wednesday's settlement ends the Miraval legal battle between Pitt and Jolie, but Pitt's case against Shefler remains.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jessica Wong is a senior digital writer in the CBC News entertainment unit, based in Toronto. You can email story tips and ideas to jessica.wong@cbc.ca.

articles.title: The US pastor who wants to see women's right to vote overturned
articles.summary: The movement to repeal women's right to vote has gained traction amongst some very conservative Christians.

blocks.text: "Patriarchy is in accordance with the way God made the world." That is the view of Pastor Doug Wilson, a conservative minister who the US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth calls his mentor.

Speaking to the BBC from his base in Moscow, Idaho, Wilson explained his view that a society led by men is "a very great blessing". It's a perspective Christians who disagree with him say is based on a fundamentalist understanding of the Bible, which promotes the subjugation of women.
A self-described Christian nationalist, Wilson believes the US should be a theocracy, with gay sex criminalised, abortion outlawed, and people of other faiths unable to hold public office.

In the past he has delivered a sermon on "The Lost Virtue of Sexism," arguing that the Bible says women should be excluded from leadership of the church, and certain roles in civic affairs. And as part of his views on the division between the sexes, he would like the 19th Amendment of the US constitution, which granted women the right to vote, to be repealed, something his detractors say is anti-democratic.
The vast majority of Christians support women's right to vote, and dismiss his message as misogynistic and extreme.
Rev. Canon Dana Colley Corsello, the vicar at the Washington National Cathedral, rejects Wilson's understanding of what the Bible says about women's roles.
"In my mind, there is no biblical precedent or standing for what [Wilson has] proposed," she told the BBC.
"I'm married, I have a husband, I have children. My husband and I are complete equals in everything we do."

items: Have the American Pope and the American administration fallen out?
Pete Hegseth brings combative style as face of Trump's war in Iran

blocks.text: But while Wilson still represents a fringe perspective amongst Christians in the US, some of his views have been gaining support.

The denomination he co-founded, the Communion of Reformed Evangelical Churches (CREC), has around 150 churches in the US. It's a drop in the ocean compared to the 350,000 or so other Christian congregations the US. But Wilson says membership continues to rise.

His influence has grown in part because of his connection to Pete Hegseth. The Secretary of Defence is a "proud member" of a CREC affiliated church, a Pentagon spokesperson told the BBC, adding that the "secretary very much appreciates many of Mr. Wilson's writings and teachings".

Wilson says the two have "a warm relationship", although he stresses it is "largely a pastoral one, not a political one". Wilson has led prayer services at the Pentagon, including one in mid-November.
Joining Wilson on stage, Pete Hegseth said "thank you for your leadership, for your mentorship, for the things you've started, the truth you've told, your willingness to be bold."
Hegseth worships at the Washington, DC branch of Wilson's network of churches. And there are other members of the current administration that worship there too, according to Wilson.
Of all his views, it is his statements on women's suffrage that have garnered the most headlines.

Wilson favours "household voting", where the head of the home – usually a man – votes on behalf of their family. It's the system used for elections within his church, although the women in Wilson's family do vote in civic elections in order to counter votes of liberals, he says.

He says only in "odd" circumstances, such as divorce or bereavement or "where the husband was a quadriplegic," should women assume the role of head of household. Just 7% of votes in Wilson's church polity are cast by women.
When challenged by the BBC, he admitted it was a system that gave men "outsized influence".
Wilson says that repealing the 19th Amendment is "low" on the list of priorities for him and his congregation. But, he adds, "we do think it".

Julie Ingersoll, a professor of religious studies at the University of North Florida, says Wilson's beliefs are misogynistic and extreme - part of a world view that says women should be in complete submission to men in every part of their lives.

It is extremely unlikely that the 19th Amendment would be repealed - it would require either a proposal from two-thirds of the House and Senate or two-thirds of the state legislatures. Three quarters of states would then need to ratify it.
Still, says Ingersoll, the threat to women's rights should be taken seriously.

"It's not unlike the battle that they waged against Roe versus Wade," she says, referencing the Supreme Court decision that granted women the right to an abortion. It was overturned in 2022, after years of legal battles that restricted women's access to abortion.
"Thirty years ago, people would have said, oh, they're not gonna undo abortion rights.
"But they chipped away and they kept chipping away until they were able to overturn it. And I see this as directly parallel."
While Wilson says overturning the 19th Amendment could take a century or more, there are conservative Christians who are pushing for women to have their right to vote removed more immediately.
Last February, pastor Dale Partridge posted on Instagram saying "We will repeal the 19th Amendment within ten years".
Partridge, who has around 900k followers across social media, credits Wilson as being someone who "broke the ice" for "strong politics and theology".
Partridge has said that "the majority of women are not capable of responsible voting" because too many of them are liberal.
He also frequently collaborates on podcasts with another conservative pastor named Joel Webbon.

Webbon, whose New Christian Right YouTube channel has more than 190k subscribers, has said that women's "desires are wicked". The solution, he claims, is to "take away women's vote". He was once friendly with Wilson, although they have since fallen out.
"Those guys have overshot by a long way," says Wilson of the two younger pastors. "They are disruptors and basically rage baiting."
So what might be driving those who support the effort?

Kelly Marino, an associate professor at Sacred Heart University who studies women's suffrage, says that the last decade has seen big wins for the women's rights movement, and "liberal political ideology" in general.
But, she argues, "any time where there was sort of this peak of feminism, there've been people who respond aggressively and try to push back".
Added to that are the high levels of uncertainty and conflict that have characterised the post-Covid period.
"I think there's been this craving for tradition and things that felt safe," Marino says.
That, she says, can be seen in the popularity of notions such as being a "tradwife" or "soft girl", who reject career goals in favour of traditionally female roles of wife and mother.

Marino says that while she doesn't think the constitution could be changed in the immediate future, the conversation around repealing the 19th Amendment is shaping the way people think about women's roles in general.
Canon Corsello, the Vicar at Washington Cathedral, sees the midterm election results as a repudiation of the push against women's rights.
"Cultural issues did not translate in this election", she says. "When people are preaching love, empathy, inclusion... that actually resonated with people".
Wilson's views have, however, been gaining ground beyond the US. The CREC has more than 30 churches internationally, including in Poland, Japan and Brazil.
The latter country has seen its own movement of right-wing influencers pressing for the removal of women's suffrage, with some leaning on religious language to make their point.
Wilson wants to continue expanding his brand of Christianity around the world, and has recently accepted a church in England into his network.
While CREC churches in each country have their own distinct characteristics, Wilson says their core beliefs are the same.

When it comes to the US, he says his ideal scenario would be for his congregations to "to practice what we believe in the church and for outsiders to look at that and envy it and say, man, that seems like a good system".

articles.title: Spanish elections: What you need to know and what's at stake
articles.summary: After eight years of Socialist-led rule, snap elections are taking place on Sunday with conservative Alberto Núñez Feijóo vying to win office.
articles.byline: Paul Kirby, Phoebe Hopson, Laura Gozzi

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
The People's Party of Alberto Núñez Feijóo is narrowly ahead in most opinion polls
ByPaul KirbyEurope digital editorPhoebe Hopson and Laura Gozzi
After eight years of Socialist-led government under Pedro Sánchez, Spain is at a crossroads.
Snap elections are taking place on Sunday 29 November, and voters face a choice of continued left-wing rule or a conservative-led government, with the likely support of far-right Vox.
Who is favourite to win?
Alberto Núñez Feijóo's conservative People's Party is narrowly ahead of the Socialist PSOE in most polls.

He has spoken of Spain being probably at "the most significant moment in our country for the past 50 years", and he aims to "repair the state, regenerate democracy, reunited the nation and recover Spain's ambition and self-esteem". But it is unlikely he could do anything without the backing of Vox, who are third in the opinion polls.
For more on Feijóo and who else to watch in this election - read here.

Spain has a population of almost 50 million, and almost 39 million people have the right to vote for the Congress and the upper house, the Senate. The polls open at 09:00 (08:00 GMT) on Sunday and close at 20:00 (19:00 GMT), when the first exit polls come out.
Why are there snap elections?
Sánchez called this vote eight months early after MPs rejected planned changes to Spain's housing laws.
He was responding to nationwide protests after an 87-year-old woman called Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her rented flat in Madrid and later died.
But his government lost the support of a centre-right party called Junts from the north-eastern region of Catalonia which sought to protect the rights of property owners.
Housing remains one of the hot-button issues for voters, but they are also focused on the high cost of living, corruption and immigration.
Why housing is so important

blocks.caption: Image caption, Spain saw its first general strike for 14 years this month over a shortage of housing and high rental costs

blocks.text: Image source, SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images
Spain saw its first general strike for 14 years this month over a shortage of housing and high rental costs
Spain's property prices and rents have soared by more than 80% from 2015 to 2025, and wages have not kept pace.
Spain has a combination of high demand and scarce supply: the Bank of Spain estimates 700,000 homes are needed to ease the pressure.

The result is that millions of Spaniards have little chance to buy a house, while they live in fear of eviction if their rent is increased. On 11 November, four million Spaniards were galvanised into joining the first general strike since 2012, according to the unions.

Pedro Sánchez has embraced housing reform as a big campaign issue and left-wing parties have promised rent controls and protection against eviction, while the right is focusing on building more homes, tax breaks for homebuyers and planning deregulation.
Does Sánchez have a chance of retaining power?

blocks.caption: Image caption, Sánchez's wife Begoña Gómez has played an important role in the election campaign

blocks.text: Sánchez's wife Begoña Gómez has played an important role in the election campaign

Support for the Socialists is down from 2023, but even then he came second in the race and relied on the backing of other parties, mainly on the left, to stay in power. This time those other left-wing parties, in particular the Broad Front (Frente Amplio) have fallen back and the big questions now are more about Feijóo's conservatives.
"It is a demobilisation of the left. Sanchez's party is not doing well," says Jacobo Ramos Folch, Policy Analyst and visiting professor at the University of Navarra.
"That lack of majority is really a reality – and the rise of Vox. What is changing that shift of majorities is the rise of Vox."
Who are Vox and what do they stand for?
Vox have been around since 2013 but polls suggest this time they could almost double their 33 seats in Spain's lower house, the Congress.

Their big themes are "national priority" – putting Spanish citizens first for subsidies and welfare, along with repatriating migrants "in an illegal situation" and "remigration" of foreigners who do not contribute to Spain.
Migration another key election issue

blocks.caption: Image caption, Pedro Sánchez (left), Alberto Núñez Feijóo (centre) and Santiago Abascal (right)

blocks.text: Pedro Sánchez (left), Alberto Núñez Feijóo (centre) and Santiago Abascal (right)

Migration has become a key challenge for Spain, and Alberto Nuñez Feijoo has accused his rival of being a "problem for Europe when it comes to immigration" after the influx of tens of thousands of migrants into the exclave of Ceuta from neighbouring Morocco in July.
This month too, the Canary Island of El Hierro has seen record arrivals, with 2,000 people landing there on 24 November. Abascal has spoken of "another invasion".
And yet a recent CIS survey put it far behind housing, cost of living, healthcare and working conditions.
The PP and Vox have bitterly criticised the Socialist-led government for a drive to legalise unauthorised migrants this year that attracted 1.2 million applications.
Feijóo's party wants to see more controlled immigration. Vox has called for mass deportations.
How corruption has hit Sánchez's government
Feijóo has accused the Socialists of being "the most corrupt party" that Spain had ever seen, and a number of cases have involved Sánchez's inner circle and family.
People should distinguish between real and "fictitious" corruption allegations, says el momento más trascendental.
His former transport minister José Luis Ábalos has been given 24 years in prison over multiple corruption offences.
Leading party figure Santos Cerdán awaits trial for alleged bribery and denies wrongdoing.

Sánchez's wife Begoña Gómez faces trial for alleged misuse of public funds and using her marriage to further her academic career. She denies wrongdoing. And his brother David Sánchez has been banned from public office for nine years for administrative misconduct.
Will the conservatives go into coalition with Vox?

Feijóo has made clear his objective is to form a majority and make "parliamentary support agreements" with Vox. As far as a coalition is concerned, he says he will respect the will of Spanish voters, but maintains Abascal has never talked to him about running any ministries.
The PP leader is clear that Vox's national priority policy would run counter to Spain's constitution and European Union treaties: "No-one can sign illegal agreements."

Even if they were to go into coalition, Camino Mortera-Martinez of the Centre for European Reform, and a former European affairs adviser to the Spanish prime minister is not convinced Vox would wield much influence.

"They're not going to get any of the core ministries. They're not going to get defence or home affairs or foreign policy or economy," she told the BBC. Even if they take over the education ministry, Mortera-Martinez argues education policy is largely devolved to Spain's regional governments.
What is Vox's record so far?

blocks.caption: Image caption, The leader of Vox, Santiago Abascal, is hoping to double his party's seats in parliament

blocks.text: Image source, Europa Press via Getty Images
The leader of Vox, Santiago Abascal, is hoping to double his party's seats in parliament

Since 2022, Vox has worked with the PP in a series of regional coalition governments, holding ministries such as culture and tourism. At the time Feijóo had reservations about Vox joining the conservatives in government in Castilla y León.

The following year they went into coalition with the conservatives in Valencia, Aragón, Murcia, and Extremadura, but pulled out of all five governments in 2024 when they refused to accept unaccompanied migrant children being moved to their regions.
They have since signed new coalition pacts with the PP in Extremadura, Aragón, Castilla y León and Andalusia.
Why are regions important in Spanish politics?

Unlike many European countries Spain has 17 autonomous communities (and two cities) that have their own parliament and their own powers. Catalonia in the north-east and the Basque Country in the north have their own police forces.
The regions matter to Sunday's result. Catalonia alone has 48 seats out of the 350 in Spain's parliament, and the Socialists have recently come to rely on regional parties for support.

Sánchez's government relied on the support of Basque separatists Bildu and two Catalan parties, ERC on the left and Junts on the right. But when Junts refused to back his housing reform, he decided to dissolve parliament.
How the election system works
Spain is made up of 50 constituencies which each have a minimum of two seats.
The exclaves of Ceuta and Melilla both have one, and the other 248 seats are divided proportionally according to voter numbers.
Madrid province will have 38 seats, Barcelona 32 and Valencia 16.
To win a seat, a party has to win 3% of the vote in a province, but in smaller provinces with fewer seats parties generally need more than that.

articles.title: France's political mainstream risks presidential vote debacle with no clear candidate
articles.summary: Hard-right and hard-left candidates dominate the polls ahead of next year's presidential election.

blocks.text: France's political mainstream faces wipe-out at the presidential election in April-May 2027, unless it acts fast to choose who it wishes to stand.

With every poll confirming the dominance of hard-right and hard-left leaders Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon, candidates of the middle-ground – the old "legacy" parties – are being squeezed out of the game.
In theory any contender from centre-right or centre-left who was chosen in the first multi-candidate round of voting in April should be in a strong position to win in the play-off a fortnight later.
That is because at their separate ends of the spectrum both Le Pen and Mélenchon have more people who oppose than support them.
But personal rivalries, lack of preparation and differing political visions have so far put paid to any hope of a meaningful challenge.
"The game in the centre is totally blocked," says political writer François Fressoz at the left-leaning Le Monde newspaper. "The partisans of reason have lost their reason."
On the left – the old Socialist Party and its acolytes – there is at least agreement on a candidate: European Parliament MP Raphaël Glucksmann.

His problem is that allies who he might once have counted on – Greens, Communists and other small left-wing parties, not to mention many Socialist voters – are being pulled inexorably into the Mélenchon orbit.

In the last two weeks, Green party leader Marine Tondelier, a majority of Communist parliamentary deputies and one-time Socialist presidential hopeful Benoît Hamon have all thrown in their lot with the leader of France Unbowed (LFI).
Another prominent figure of the left – François Ruffin – has also withdrawn from the race, bowing to the unbowed Mélenchon's now almost total command of the field.

So with the soft-left emasculated, the main hope for an alternative to Le Pen and Mélenchon has to be focused on the right. But here the prospects – which until recently seemed bright – are now clouded with gloom.
"A Mélenchon–Le Pen duel in round two is not yet inevitable," says Guillaume Tabard, political analyst at the conservative Le Figaro newspaper. "But it is looking increasingly probable."

In recent weeks the poll ratings of the main centre-right hopeful Edouard Philippe – a former prime minister under President Macron – have fallen sharply, and he is now consistently placed behind Mélenchon in the first round of the vote. Marine Le Pen is way ahead of both.

Other candidates for command of this centre-right "space" are circling. They include another former Macron prime minister, Gabriel Attal; the leader of the right-wing Republicans (and former Macron interior minister), Bruno Retailleau; and now – a surprise new challenger – the mayor of Cannes, David Lisnard.

Lisnard, who stands on a liberal economic platform of less state and lower taxes, has emerged from nowhere to become the man of the hour. Membership of his micro-party Nouvelle Energie (New Energy) has shot up to more than 100,000, and he is being taken seriously as a possible Philippe replacement.

But this very multiplicity of names – not to mention others like judoka Teddy Riner, journalist Natacha Polony and former prime minister Dominique de Villepin – betrays the essential weakness of the centre-right challenge.

According to veteran commentator Nicolas Baverez, "If you want to win an election, it's quite simple: you need a strategy, a programme, and activists. Right now in the space between Le Pen and Mélenchon we have none of that: there is a total vacuum.
"The most glaring absence is digital. Mélenchon especially, but Le Pen too, are running extremely effective social media campaigns. In the middle… nothing."
Guillaume Tabard agrees that the lack of a shared platform is proving a serious handicap.
"In recent weeks we have seen Marine Le Pen issue her manifesto proposals for reforming pensions. We have seen Jean-Luc Mélenchon publish his programme in a best-selling book," he says.
"What do we have in between? Arguments about names and polling figures and whether or not there should be a primary. It's not, to put it mildly, an encouraging start."

For Fressoz, "There is no-one in the centre who is taking up the fight. When Le Pen makes her proposals about pensions, there is no-one saying, 'Hang on, that doesn't add up!'. Macron – who did after all take her on and beat her – is said to be furious."

Any mention of Macron, though, is most unwelcome for the camp that nominally is his heir. Philippe, Attal and Retailleau all served under a president who Baverez now calls "as toxic as Trump", so deep is his unpopularity in the country. Lisnard, by contrast, makes much of his refusal to serve under Macron – but he faces another handicap.

According to Fressoz, "Lisnard has shot up in the polls because he is on the right of the right, and there is always an appetite for a figure who is not Le Pen, but who speaks her kind of language on immigration.
"But Lisnard is an economic liberal, and in France that is a minority taste. He'll have his moment but then he will deflate."

With five months to go to until the election, all is not lost for the mainstream. Optimists in its ranks say that come the new year, opinion polls will start settling behind one or other centre-right candidate, and the others will feel obliged to step aside.

Talk of a centre-right primary – as occurred ahead of the 2017 election – is beginning to ebb. The two strongest candidates, Philippe and Lisnard, are opposed. Lisnard says he supports one but his conditions are designed to be unacceptable to the rest. Retailleau and Attal are in favour – but that, says Tabard, is "mainly as a way to keep their hopes alive."

In theory then it is possible a name will emerge in January or February, and start pulling behind him (or less likely, her) the mass of voters who do not want a disruptive radical as France's next head of state.
Possible, but hardly a good bet.
For Fressoz of Le Monde, "After years of Macron's 'neither left nor right', the left and right are once again shaping French politics. But now it is the extremes who are in control."

Le Pen and Mélenchon have both already run three times for the presidency. Their visions were defined long ago, their strategies laid, their activists trained. Polarisation is their friend, so is the social tension of recent weeks, and both are undisputed masters in their own camps.
The 2027 dénouement has been in their sights for years. That is their massive advantage.

articles.title: Has global jihadism failed, or is it simply changing shape?
articles.summary: Jihadist groups appear to be focusing on local issues rather than global terror. Does it signify a real change?

blocks.text: ByMina al-Lami
Chief jihadist media specialist, BBC Monitoring

blocks.caption: Mina al-Lami

blocks.text: Rice, pasta, sugar, cooking oil and beans are hardly what you'd expect to see in jihadist propaganda. Yet these were among the supplies that al-Qaeda's Somali branch, al-Shabab, said its "charity" had handed out to hundreds of struggling families in August, as it publicised the aid through its social media accounts and radio station.
The group, which controls large parts of rural southern and central Somalia, has been keen to show off its so-called humanitarian work throughout 2026.
"May God reward them," said a local woman in one of al-Shabab's videos.
It's all part of an effort to win over local communities and present itself as more than just a jihadist group.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Al-Shabab has been publicising its humanitarian work

blocks.text: Image source, Telegram
Al-Shabab has been publicising its humanitarian work

A quarter of a century after al-Qaeda's 9/11 attacks in the US, and 12 years after Islamic State group (IS) declared its so-called caliphate in Iraq and Syria, the jihadist movement looks very different.

Rather than focusing on attacking the West or fighting for a global Islamic state, some - especially those linked to al-Qaeda - are putting more effort into winning power closer to home. And they seem increasingly willing to make compromises along the way.

Because of this, a debate is growing within the movement. While hardliners reject compromise, pragmatists see working with local groups and former enemies as a way to gain power. But do the pragmatists represent a genuine change or simply a shift in tactics to achieve the same ultimate goals: establishing a state that applies their strict interpretation of Islamic Sharia law both at home and in its dealings with the outside world?
Significant defeats
Neither al-Qaeda nor IS has achieved its ultimate dream: taking over one or more countries and ruling them according to their strict interpretation of Islam.

Both have suffered major defeats, lost leaders and faced years of international pressure. IS, which once controlled vast areas of Iraq and Syria, lost its last territorial stronghold in 2019. But jihadism hasn't gone away.

Africa is now the main battleground for jihadism, with al-Qaeda's powerful branches, JNIM in the Sahel (Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger) and al-Shabab in Somalia, fighting long-running insurgencies. IS, its bitter rival, has active branches in Nigeria, the Democratic Republic of Congo, the Sahel, Mozambique and Somalia.

One major source of inspiration, and envy, whether jihadists admit it or not, is Syria's new president, Ahmed al-Sharaa. The former IS and then al-Qaeda commander was once wanted by the US but rose to power in Syria in December 2024 and was welcomed by Western leaders.
Once known by his militant nom de guerre Abu Mohammed al-Jolani, he led the jihadist group Nusra Front - initially linked to IS and then al-Qaeda - and later the group Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS).
He gradually broke ties with both IS and al-Qaeda and distanced himself from their calls for global jihad.
Instead, he focused on Syria, building a local power base in the north-western Idlib province.

What surprised everyone was his growing willingness to work with non-Islamist groups and engage with foreign powers. As HTS advanced on Damascus, its leadership sought to reassure the international community, reaching out even to Russia, a key ally of then-president Bashar al-Assad, to allay fears of an Islamist takeover.
That pragmatism, combined with favourable geopolitical conditions - including a weaker Russia and Iran - helped him take power in Syria.
But the sight of him being welcomed by world leaders, including US President Donald Trump, was even more remarkable.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Trump joked with Sharaa when he visited the White House

blocks.text: Image source, AP
Trump joked with Sharaa when he visited the White House
During Sharaa's visit to the White House in November 2025, Trump sprayed him with his own branded cologne, jokingly asked how many wives he had and praised him as a "very strong leader".
For some jihadists, Sharaa's success has been inspiring. Others, however, see his actions as a betrayal of everything they believe in.

IS has declared jihad against Syria's new Islamist government, branding Sharaa and his officials "apostates", and has carried out attacks against government forces on that basis. Other hardline clerics have taken a similar stance, but have stopped short of openly calling for jihad against Sharaa.

The divide between hardline jihadists and their more pragmatic counterparts has fuelled a bitter online debate since 2025, with rival voices trading accusations of betrayal and even publishing competing books to defend their positions.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Sharaa, centre, in 2016, was once a jihadist leader wanted by the FBI

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Sharaa, centre, in 2016, was once a jihadist leader wanted by the FBI

For hardliners, going too far can mean abandoning their core beliefs. This might include holding back from imposing their strict version of Islamic law, accepting "man-made" laws or a constitution, taking part in elections, working with non-Islamist groups, or building ties with governments they consider "infidel".

Another source of inspiration for jihadists was the Taliban's return to power in Afghanistan in 2021, as it showed that an Islamist movement could eventually take control of a country after years of fighting Western-backed forces. It engaged local groups, slowly secured power across the country, used international diplomacy, and bided its time before taking the capital, Kabul, in a lightning offensive.
A means to an end?
Two groups are especially worth watching: al-Qaeda's branches in Mali and Somalia.

In late April, al-Qaeda's Sahel branch, known as JNIM, showed considerable pragmatism by joining forces with nationalist Tuareg separatists - whom it had occasionally fought - to launch a major offensive that threatened Mali's military rulers. It even went as far as to call the Tuaregs "brothers".
But it's not just JNIM's growing military strength that's attracting attention. It's also how the group is presenting itself.
Its propaganda once prominently featured al-Qaeda's leaders, slogans and calls for global jihad. Since late 2024, however, its videos have dropped the familiar al-Qaeda branding.
And instead of talking about global Muslim causes, JNIM has increasingly focused on local problems, portraying itself as a defender of ordinary people against corrupt and abusive rulers.
It has repeatedly accused Mali's military government and its Russian allies of killing civilians and making people's lives worse.
In April, it appealed to "all sincere patriots" to help build a "new Mali", promising security, justice and prosperity alongside Islamic law.

It has even suggested it could have "balanced relations" with Russia, despite the fact they're fighting Russian forces backing Mali's government. Its wording echoed that of HTS to Russia as it advanced on Damascus.
There are parallels with Sharaa's approach in Syria: build local alliances, reassure potential enemies and avoid giving outside powers a reason to intervene.
Africa security specialist Aman Bezreh sees similarities between the two groups, but says JNIM's shift may take time.

"JNIM has indeed shown signs of pragmatism similar to HTS", she says. "However, its rebranding has progressed more slowly because the group is simultaneously focused on expanding into new territories and recruiting from diverse pools."
Taliban v Sharaa
The debate over which path to follow is also taking place within JNIM's leadership, according to Wassim Nasr, a France 24 journalist and jihadism expert.

He says one camp favours the Taliban's approach of taking power through force with minimal concessions. The other, which he says currently has the upper hand, favours an approach closer to that of Syria's HTS - making compromises and building wider alliances to gain power more quickly.
Nasr believes JNIM may borrow from both models, but that a break with al-Qaeda is inevitable as a result of its political evolution.
Like JNIM, al-Shabab in Somalia appears willing to make deals with former enemies.

According to Abdullahi Guji, BBC Monitoring's Somalia specialist, al-Shabab reached a truce in October with a powerful Somali tribe, the Ma'awisley, whose fighters had been at the forefront of the fight against the group.
The tribe has since withdrawn its fighters from the front line, dealing a serious blow to the government's campaign against jihadists, says Guji.
Guji believes the group may soon have a chance to test whether it can seize power and establish itself as an alternative government across wider parts of the country.

African Union forces are withdrawing from Somalia amid funding cuts and the approaching end of their mandate in December. Meanwhile, the Somali government is facing political crises and rebellions, creating vulnerabilities al-Shabab could exploit, he adds.
There's another reason some jihadists may see an opportunity to expand: they believe Western governments have bigger fish to fry.
With the war in Ukraine, US-Iran conflict in the Middle East and growing rivalries with China and Russia, fighting jihadists is no longer the priority it was after 9/11.
The US withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021 and the Taliban's return to power, followed by Sharaa's rise in Syria, have reinforced that belief.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The Taliban has inspired many jihadists

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
The Taliban has inspired many jihadists

Colin Clarke, executive director of the Soufan Center, a non-profit research group that focuses on security, says some jihadist groups have learnt that avoiding confrontation with the US can help them escape Western military action and "live to fight another day".
That doesn't mean the West has stopped fighting terrorism. But if jihadists believe it is distracted or less willing to intervene, they may feel emboldened to pursue power.
History lessons
Unlike its fiercely uncompromising rival IS, al-Qaeda has long shown some flexibility in pursuing its goals. But history offers a warning.

After the 2011 Arab uprisings, which largely sidelined al-Qaeda, affiliated jihadist groups in Yemen, Libya and Tunisia began using the name Ansar al-Sharia (Supporters of Sharia) to win local support without carrying the al-Qaeda brand.

In Mali in 2012, al-Qaeda leaders advised jihadists who had seized the north alongside Tuareg separatists not to rush into imposing strict Islamic rules. Instead, they urged them to work with local allies, avoid alienating communities and play down their al-Qaeda links.
The message wasn't to give up their ambitions. It was to show strategic patience until the time was right. That same thinking could be at work today.

So are these groups really changing their ambitions, or just their tactics? Even those advocating compromise aren't necessarily abandoning their dream of establishing a state ruled by their strict interpretation of Islamic law.
Clarke wonders whether this more pragmatic approach could be a "Trojan horse strategy" – a way for jihadist groups to gain power without giving up their longer-term goals.
"The big question is whether being in power actually moderates these groups, or whether they're simply changing their tactics to survive and strengthen their position," he says.
But not everyone is changing tactics.

IS remains firmly committed to its global ambitions and rejects compromise. Al-Qaeda's Yemen branch, AQAP, continues to call for attacks against the US and Israel, and urges "lone wolf" attacks against Western and Jewish targets.
And it's too early to say whether groups like JNIM and al-Shabab will follow the Taliban or Syrian examples, and whether they're willing to make compromises.
Some jihadist groups may become more focused on local politics as they face the challenges of governing. Others may simply be hiding their wider ambitions until they're strong enough to pursue them.
The global jihadist dream may have failed, but jihadism is far from finished.

articles.title: Duran Duran guitarist and songwriter Andy Taylor dies at 65
articles.summary: 'To the world, Andy was a brilliant guitarist, but to us, he was the most wonderful husband, a loving dad and the proudest grandfather,' says Taylor's wife, Tracy Wilson-Taylor

blocks.text: DURAN DURAN. Members of British band Duran Duran (from left) Andy Taylor, Roger Taylor, Simon Le Bon, Nick Rhodes and John Taylor arrive at the 2003 MTV Video Music Awards in Radio City Music Hall in New York in this August 28, 2003 file photo.
'To the world, Andy was a brilliant guitarist, but to us, he was the most wonderful husband, a loving dad and the proudest grandfather,' says Taylor's wife, Tracy Wilson-Taylor

items: Andy Taylor, guitarist and songwriter for Duran Duran, passed away at 65 due to metastatic prostate cancer, which he was diagnosed with in 2018.
He co-wrote major hits for the band, including 'Hungry Like the Wolf' and 'Rio,' and was remembered by his family and bandmates for his talent and personal qualities.
Born in 1961, Taylor joined Duran Duran in 1980, contributing significantly to their early success and later pursued a solo career.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

LOS ANGELES, USA – Andy Taylor, the guitarist and songwriter for pop-rock band Duran Duran and a Rock and Roll Hall of Fame inductee, died at age 65 on Monday, according to a joint statement from his family and former bandmates released on Wednesday, November 25.
Taylor, who co-wrote some of the group’s biggest hits, including “Hungry Like the Wolf,” “Rio,” and “Girls on Film,” died from metastatic prostate cancer. He was diagnosed in 2018.
The first section of the statement came from his family, while the second was from Duran Duran members Simon Le Bon, Nick Rhodes, John Taylor and Roger Taylor.

“To the world, Andy was a brilliant guitarist, but to us, he was the most wonderful husband, a loving dad and the proudest grandfather,” Taylor’s wife, Tracy Wilson-Taylor, said on behalf of his family.
The members of the Grammy-winning band noted that Taylor brought a unique style to their sound.

“Andy was there at the very beginning of our story. From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music,” they said, adding that he faced his illness with courage, honesty and grace.

Born in 1961 in Tynemouth and raised in Cullercoats, Northumberland, Taylor began learning guitar at age 11 and later dropped out of school to tour England and Europe with several bands. He moved to Birmingham and joined Duran Duran in 1980.
The group signed with EMI Records and released its debut album, “Duran Duran,” in 1981. While the record was successful in the United Kingdom, global fame followed with 1982’s “Rio.”
Taylor later launched a solo career, releasing his debut studio album, “Thunder,” in 1987.
The late musician has four children with Wilson-Taylor. – Rappler.com
