articles.title: Sri Lankan asylum seeker killed himself after being sent by UK to Eswatini
articles.summary:
Kishanth Peramalya was denied entry due to sexual assault convictions and sent to Africa where he had no connections

The UK sent a Sri Lankan asylum seeker who had been convicted of sexual…

blocks.text: The UK sent a Sri Lankan asylum seeker who had been convicted of sexual assault to Eswatini, a southern African country to which he had no connection and where he killed himself.

Kishanth Peramalya was part of a group that set sail from India hoping to reach Canada and claim asylum there. The boat was rescued by the Royal Navy in October 2021 when it got into difficulty and brought to Diego Garcia in the remote British Indian Ocean Territory, which hosts a US-UK military base.

In November 2024, the UK allowed 61 migrants to enter from Diego Garcia after a damning UN report about conditions in the camp. However, the then home secretary, Yvette Cooper, denied Peramalya entry to the UK due to his criminal convictions while he was on Diego Garcia for four counts of sexual assault, one count of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and one count of arson. Cooper’s decision was upheld by UK courts.

Peramalya had been granted protection from being returned to Sri Lanka, having been tortured and sexually abused by Sri Lankan military personnel as a teenager. In late March, the Maldives said it would take him for 30 days, according to the BBC. He was then transferred to Eswatini, a country landlocked by South Africa and Mozambique and formerly known as Swaziland, where he killed himself on 13 September.

A draft deal between the UK and Eswatini governments would have committed Downing Street to cover the costs of Peramalya’s resettlement there for three years, according to the BBC, which said the UK was also finalising arrangements for Peramalya to live in Eswatini permanently.

The Guardian has not seen the draft deal. Thabile Mdluli, a spokesperson for Eswatini’s government, said: “The initial arrangement was temporary in nature and intended to safeguard Mr Peramalya’s safety while the government of the United Kingdom worked towards a long-term solution regarding his circumstances.”

She said that no formal agreement was ever reached over Peramalya’s long-term residency status with the UK and declined to comment further on the specific arrangements of his stay in Eswatini or the circumstances around his death.

Mdluli said: “Eswatini has not received any other similar request from the government of the United Kingdom. The government of the Kingdom of Eswatini remains committed to ensuring that any agreements entered into with external partners safeguard national interest as well as the safety and security of Emaswati [Swazi people].”

A UK government spokesperson said: “Keeping the British public safe will always be our first priority, and we will continue to take the decisions necessary to protect the British people. That includes taking steps to ensure high harm foreign criminals cannot enter the UK. We continue to work with the Eswatini authorities in relation to this case.”
Peramalya had post-traumatic stress disorder and attempted suicide multiple times on Diego Garcia, according to a UK high court judgment in February 2025.

Peramalya’s family told the BBC he was initially housed alone in an isolated guesthouse in Eswatini. “My brother did not want to go there at all,” said his sister, speaking from India. “He couldn’t manage being there alone, he was very lonely.”
after newsletter promotion

She said he had called her four times a day and was initially having weekly psychiatric appointments, which were made daily when his mental health deteriorated, as well as having someone brought in to prepare his food.
Peramalya’s relatives said they were not aware of his convictions for sexual offences or any plan to make his transfer to Eswatini permanent.

Eswatini has accepted dozens of third-country deportees from the US since July 2025. In November 2025, its government confirmed it had received $5.1m in exchange for taking up to 160 migrants from the US.

articles.title: Indian Cockroach movement leader asks court for permission to fly to UK
articles.summary:
Officials at Delhi airport stopped Saurav Das from boarding flight to Britain, where students have invited him to speak

A leader of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement has asked the Delhi…

blocks.text: A leader of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement has asked the Delhi high court to give him permission to fly to the UK after immigration officials at Delhi airport stopped him boarding a flight early on Tuesday morning.

The court is scheduled to hear Saurav Das’s case on Thursday morning. His lawyer asked the court for a quick hearing because Das has by now already missed some of his engagements at British universities and can only attend the other events on his itinerary if he is allowed to fly out as soon as possible.
Das, 27, is one of the main faces of the Cockroach movement, which shot into the political firmament out of nowhere in May to challenge the Narendra Modi government with street protests.
The movement succeeded in forcing the education minister to resign in July over exam leaks and has since functioned as a pressure group.
Das had been invited by the Oxford Union Society to participate in a “fireside chat” on the movement.
Indian student groups at Edinburgh, Cambridge, Queen Mary University of London and the London School of Economics have also invited him to speak.
“Students want to know how we succeeded without any violence, how we began and where we are going. There is a great curiosity about the movement,” Das told the Guardian.
Reports in the Indian media have alleged that Das was informed well before the flight that his passport contained discrepancies.

“None of these reports is true,” said Das. “I received an email five hours before my flight saying that I should not use my passport for travel. It gave no reason. And I did not see the email until I arrived at Delhi airport. What’s more, I’ve travelled abroad before on this passport since it was issued in 2019 so what’s the problem with it now?”

He suspects that the government is using a frivolous case filed in Chennai against him as a pretext. The case has been filed, Das surmises, by someone hostile to the Cockroach movement and disputes his citizenship.

Das believes he was deliberately stopped by a government that is “scared” of someone such as him speaking abroad about the ideals of Mahatma Gandhi and Jawaharlal Nehru (independent India’s first prime minister) and that it wanted to make an example of him.
“It’s a chilling signal to young Indians that we can do what we like, that if we can do this to a leader of a movement, we can do this to you too,” said Das.
after newsletter promotion
In recent years, the government has stopped foreign speakers and academics, including several from the UK, from entering India.

Last year, Francesca Orsini, a professor at Soas University of London, was stopped at Delhi airport and deported despite holding a valid visa. The government said she had been blacklisted for allegedly conducting research and speaking at events while visiting on a tourist visa in 2024.
Also last year, Nitasha Kaul, a professor at Westminster University, was detained at Bangalore airport and deported for “anti-India activities”.

Some people who find themselves blacklisted have chosen to fight back. In 2023, the UK-based journalist Amrit Wilson had her overseas citizen of India card which allows free movement into India cancelled, also for alleged “anti-India activities”.
She took legal action and earlier this week, the Delhi high court ruled that the government had failed to give any concrete details of what it meant by “anti-India activities”.
The court has given the government a week to issue a fresh notice, this time giving specific reasons.

articles.title: Man, 39, killed in midtown Toronto invasion was musician
articles.summary: A man killed in a midtown Toronto home invasion early Wednesday is being remembered as a talented musician who "always led with his heart," according to a longtime friend. Police have identified the…

blocks.text: Toronto

A man killed in a midtown Toronto home invasion early Wednesday is being remembered as a talented musician who "always led with his heart," according to a longtime friend. Police have identified the man as Michael Eckert, 39.
Michael Eckert was confronted by a suspect before he was shot, police say
Victim in fatal home invasion was Toronto musician
A man killed in a midtown Toronto home invasion early Wednesday is being remembered as a talented musician who "always led with his heart," according to a longtime friend.
Police have identified the man who was fatally shot as Michael Eckert, 39.

Emergency crews responded to reports of a shooting at a residence in the St. Clair Avenue West and Poplar Plains Road area at around 2:40 a.m., according to a Toronto police news release Wednesday afternoon.

An unknown number of suspects forced entry into the residence, police said. One of the suspects was confronted by Eckert, shot him and fled the home, police said. Eckert was taken to hospital, where he was pronounced dead.
Staff Sgt. Shain Griffin with 53 Division told CBC News early Wednesday morning the victim was the homeowner's son.
Police identified the victim of a shooting during a home invasion in midtown Toronto Wednesday as Michael Eckert, 39, of Toronto. (Toronto Police Service)
Toronto police Det. Sgt. Alan Bartlett said at a news conference earlier Wednesday that there is no evidence to suggest the family was targeted.
"I understand and recognize how deeply troubling this must be, not only to the residents of that community, but to the residents of the city of Toronto as a whole," Bartlett said.
There were four residents inside the home at the time but no one else was injured, he said.
This is Toronto's 37th homicide of the year, according to police.
Bartlett said Toronto police Chief Myron Demkiw assured him that every resource available will be provided to investigators and "no expense will be spared."
He said police do not yet have details on the number of suspects, any descriptions or what vehicles may have been used.
He urged anyone with surveillance video or anyone who saw anything between 2 a.m. and 3 a.m. to contact police.
Residents on edge after man killed during attempted home invasion
Victim was a 'loving and caring person': friend

Galen Pelley, a friend of Eckert, said he knew him for about 20 years after they met studying music at Humber College. He said they made music together ever since they met and he felt Eckert was like a brother to him.
"We're all still in shock," Pelley said Wednesday. "We can't believe that this would happen to anyone, let alone someone that we all cared about and who cared for so many himself."
Pelley said Eckert, the youngest child in his family, had two sisters and two brothers and did more than his share of taking care of others. He was also an uncle, he said.
"Mike always led with his heart, both on stage and off stage," he said. "He had an affinity for drummers and I always thought guitarists wrote the best songs."
Friend of fatal home invasion victim says Michael was ‘chosen family’
Pelley described Eckert as a "gentle giant" who was an avid reader and a humble, "loving and caring person."
"He spoke louder through his music than he ever would off stage or in person," he said.
Eckert's instrument of choice was the pedal steel guitar, he said.
Eckert performed at the 113th Grey Cup in Calgary as back up for Blue Rodeo this month, Pelley said, adding: "He's gone too soon and that was a real moment for him to flourish."
'Far too many' home invasions in Toronto: city councillor
Coun. Josh Matlow told reporters outside the home Wednesday there have been "far too many" home invasions in the city and that it needs to be a top priority to address residents' concerns.

"There's a feeling amongst Torontonians that far too often people go to bed at night worrying about whether or not they'll wake up to somebody in their home," Matlow said, adding there's work to do in the community to support "very scared" residents.
He said he has offered Demkiw his "complete support" during the investigation. He urged people to not jump to conclusions.
MPP Stephanie Smyth, who joined Matlow, said police do what they can to investigate incidents, but that more needs to be done to address the fear residents feel.

Coun. Josh Matlow and MPP Stephanie Smyth spoke to reporters outside the scene of a fatal home invasion on Wednesday. They shared their condolences for the victim's loved ones and reassured residents they will do their best to address fears. (Paul Smith/CBC)
"They can talk about the stats all they want, but the bottom line is people are afraid. And the one place you should not feel afraid is in your own home," she said.

Matlow added that "it's shameful" to hear that many residents in the neighbourhood and nearby areas have hired private security to safeguard their homes. Smyth said there needs to be stronger deterrence for such crimes, such as harsher penalties.
"People have to do what they feel is the right choice to ensure the safety of their family," Bartlett said in regards to some people hiring private security.

When asked what tips he had for residents regarding a potential home invasion, he said people should call 911 immediately and that Toronto Police Service "provides the best that it can in terms of public safety services."
"Oftentimes we can't provide the why, we simply don't know. What my promise has been to the victims' family is that we'll do our very best to provide the who."
Incident follows Bridle Path home invasion last month

The incident comes nearly a month after a home invasion and shooting sent a family of four adults in Toronto's Bridle Path neighbourhood to hospital. Police arrested one suspect in Ottawa last week and are looking for two others.

Police have been investigating and patrolling to deter home invasions in parts of the city after seeing a rise in incidents earlier this year, Demkiw said in remarks to the Toronto Police Service Board back in July.

items: 4 hospitalized as Toronto police investigate home invasion, shooting at Bridle Path home
Here's where home invasions are happening in Toronto and what's being done to prevent them

blocks.text: He said the service launched the initiative in areas that saw the largest increase in home invasions, which includes 22, 32 and 53 Divisions. The 22 division covers neighbourhoods in central and southern Etobicoke, 32 operates in central and western North York, and 53 Division covers central and midtown Toronto.
"We continue to put our people and our resources where we see challenges, and where we hear concerns from our communities," Demkiw told the police board.

Home invasions hit a 10-year high in 2024, before dropping in 2025 and then rising again at the beginning of this year in Toronto, according to CBC News analysis of Toronto police data. Affluent areas with large detached houses and driveways were among the hardest hit.
With files from Eleanor Yuneun Park, Dale Manucdoc and The Canadian Press

articles.title: China misusing Interpol to target dissidents, says leading UK lawyer
articles.summary:
Concerns over Beijing’s use of ‘red notices’ as Hong Kong prepares to host police organisation’s general assembly

China is misusing Interpol to target and silence dissidents, a leading…

blocks.text: China is misusing Interpol to target and silence dissidents, a leading British lawyer has claimed, as Hong Kong prepares to host the police organisation’s general assembly for the first time.

Ben Keith, a specialist in “red notices” - the Interpol system under which national authorities are requested to locate and detain suspects - said he was working on five cases involving China making questionable requests through Interpol.

He revealed that he had also contacted officials at the law enforcement organisation in July on behalf of a group of five high-profile UK-based Chinese dissidents to find out if Beijing had sought the issuance of red notices relating to them.

Interpol responded in October that they were looking into his request for information but there had been no substantive information shared, he added, raising concerns that there might be data relating to the individuals on the Interpol system.

He said: “If there’s no data, than they will tell me there’s no data. If there is data, then they have to get permission from Hong Kong to tell me. It has been sometime now. Given the profile of these individuals, I think they may have had some data on them. That’s the fear.”

Many Hong Kong democracy campaigners who fled to the UK in recent years have British national (overseas) status but this does not protect them from red notices outside the UK and potential extradition to China.

A red notice is a request to law enforcement worldwide to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition, surrender, or similar legal action. It is based on an arrest warrant or court order issued by the judicial authorities in the requesting country. Member countries apply their own laws in deciding whether to arrest a person.

Keith said: “The Russian playbook was to accuse political opponents or business opponents of some sort of really technical criminal offence of fraud, employment law breach, regulatory offence, that sort of thing, to disguise the real purpose of the request. The Chinese have taken that on.”

Hong Kong will host the 94th Interpol general assembly between 30 November and 3 December, attracting police chiefs from its 196 member countries to set global policing policy, approve budgets and activities, and pass binding resolutions.

Keith said that hosting the assembly offered an opportunity for China to “reputation wash”, arguing that Beijing ran a sophisticated public relations machine to hide the high proportion of red notice and extradition requests that were politically motivated.

The red notice system is used by China to target those sought under the state campaigns launched under President Xi Jinping to track down fugitives overseas and recover illicit funds, known as Operations Fox Hunt and Sky Net, it is claimed.

A new report, The Red Notice Trap, by Ben Keith and Rhys Davies of the legal firm IHR Advisors, draws on court judgments, Interpol records and Chinese-language official documents, to show how red notices fit into Beijing’s campaign to silence critics and bring them home for persecution.

It notes under a 2025 revision of the implementing regulations for the People’s Repubilc of China’s supervision law that red notice requests sit with extradition, judicial assistance, law enforcement cooperation, prosecution abroad, asset seizure and ‘ideological education’, as tools for the recovery of people.

blocks.caption: Yidiresi Aishan, AKA Idris Hassan, a Uyghur activist, was detained after a red notice was issued by Interpol at China’s request.  Photograph: AP

blocks.text: Among the cases cited in the IHR Advisors report is that of Yidiresi Aishan – a Uyghur activist who is also known as Idris Hassan – who was arrested in July 2021, when arriving at Casablanca airport on a flight from Turkey, where he had been living.

He was detained on the basis of a red notice issued by Interpol at China’s request “for belonging to a terrorist organisation”. Within two weeks, Interpol suspended the notice as it breached its rules and it was later cancelled.
The Moroccan extradition proceedings carried on regardless and in December 2021 the country’s court of cassation approved Hasan’s surrender to China.

The UN committee against torture found that Hasan’s extradition would breach article 3 of the convention against torture and Morocco did not carry out the extradition But Hasan remained in detention until 12 February 2025 after spending nearly four years in prison on the basis of an Interpol red notice.
“His case shows the central weakness this report returns to: Interpol can correct its own data, but it cannot undo what national authorities have already set in motion”, the authors write.
Hasan, who now lives in Canada, said he no longer travelled and that his life had been thrown “upside down”.
“Four years of life have gone, just spent in prison, I could not be with my children,” he told the Guardian. “Everything has changed. I cannot describe this. But I trust Canada.”
Hasan added: “I don’t understand how this kind of the big organisation like Interpol how they took my name down without evidence, without nothing. Just put my name out.”
Interpol and the Chinese embassy have been approached for comment.

articles.title: Pro-Palestine activist sought by US in extradition case: ‘I still have a right to my beliefs’
articles.summary:
James ‘Fergie’ Chambers, at center of legal fight, says he ‘should not be unjustly accused’ because of leftwing views

James “Fergie” Chambers, the wealthy leftwing activist and donor…

blocks.text: James “Fergie” Chambers, the wealthy leftwing activist and donor controversially sought in extradition by the US, has told the Guardian that he is “not asking anyone to endorse my ideas or not think I’m a jerk – but I still have a right to my beliefs and should not be unjustly accused because of them”.

Chambers’s case is the first known instance of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation apparently tied to an international money-laundering charge in the criminal complaint underpinning the extradition request and donations to organizations helping Palestinians in Gaza.
The complaint also includes riot and conspiracy to riot charges stemming from 2023 protests against New England branches of Israeli weapons manufacturer Elbit.

Chambers was speaking from his Madrid apartment in his first in-depth interview after a Spanish appeals court ordered his provisional release on bail on Friday. That release was due to issues with the legally required US translation of the extradition request’s core documents into Spanish, first reported by the Guardian.
“Support for my case doesn’t imply support of me, or my ideas,” Chambers said. “It’s about my right to have those ideas – and not be falsely accused of things.”
Chambers, whose case has gained attention across the world, had been detained since 10 July, when Spanish authorities arrested him in Ibiza.

The order granting Chambers’s provisional release asserted that the translation issues cause “a diminishment, at least for the time being, in the solidity or foundation of the extradition request”. Spanish judges had previously denied bail three times.

The wealthy heir to at least $250mn from his family’s business – Atlanta–based Cox Enterprises – was in the middle of his first visit without being separated by glass with his mother, Lauren Hamilton, when he was summoned to receive the “good news” on Friday, Chambers told the Guardian.

Minutes later, he returned to tell his mother he was being released. “She freaked out crying. We went nuts for about five minutes. Then we got to contacting my lawyer and getting my kids on a plane to Spain.”
On Monday, Chambers’s five-year-old son with actor and activist Stella Schnabel could be heard in the background. The tableau was in stark contrast to his months in prison.

“I tried to build a cocoon to deal with the immense unknown, the immense fear,” he said of his time in Aranjuez prison. “I would pray a lot. The only idea I could hold onto was, my home is the truth. The truth of who loves you. The truth of my own innocence. And the truth of what is happening in Palestine and all the things connected to what is happening in Palestine – other wars, gas prices. No one can take that away from you.”

blocks.caption: Stella Schnabel, Chambers’s wife, and lawyer Baltasar Garzon speak to the media in Madrid in September. Photograph: Eduardo Parra/Europa Press/Getty Images

blocks.text: Chambers has been supported by his mother throughout his case, and has reconnected with his father, James Cox Chambers – who owns an estimated 17% stake in Cox Enterprises but does not play an active role in the company – for the first time in five years.
“Speaking with my parents has provided emotional stability – and intelligent, adult minds to help make decisions,” Chambers said.

Although he has had political disagreements with his father, a donor to the Democratic party, Chambers said his father “sees this situation as totally unthinkable and out of step with anything resembling a just society”.
He also invoked his grandfather, the ACLU civil rights lawyer James Cox Hamilton, who died in 2014. “He would’ve turned in his grave over this,” Chambers said.

While locked up, Chambers, a US citizen, received hundreds of letters of support from friends, family and strangers, postmarked from Atlanta to Barcelona – including, he said, “from a guy who had been imprisoned under [Spanish dictator Francisco] Franco, who painted the ‘key of return’ [a symbol of homes lost in the 1948 Nakba] on the Palestinian flag”.

Chambers’s views and donations to progressive and humanitarian projects have been extensively profiled in US media, including his controversial public comments on Israel and Gaza. A week after the 7 October Hamas attacks on Israel, he posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/It’s simply genocide/Like it has been.”
after newsletter promotion

His release followed a separate decision on Thursday by a three-judge panel at Spain’s high court tasked with deciding on the extradition to pause the proceedings in order to evaluate the impact of the alterations the US made to the original, machine-made translation of the extradition request into Spanish.

The US admitted to making several of the changes, calling them “substantial [and] inadvertent”. These and dozens of other changes introduced prejudicial notions with specific legal implications that in turn wound up in the Spanish prosecutor’s report on the case, Aitor Martínez, a member of Chambers’s defense team, told the Guardian last week.

It was also recently revealed that there is no indictment behind the complaint, meaning the federal government has not had a grand jury evaluate evidence against Chambers, and instead is seeking his extradition based on the affidavit of a single FBI agent, the core of the sealed criminal complaint.

During his time in prison, Chambers also began the process of applying for political asylum in Spain. He cannot be extradited until the asylum case runs its course, and also cannot be extradited if he is granted asylum. His legal team has notified the government office evaluating his asylum petition of the altered translations.

Chambers was arrested 10 July as he and Schnabel pulled into the driveway of a school they were visiting to see about enrolling their five-year-old, part of plans to move to Spain. They had been staying in Ireland, where Schnabel was working on a film.

Although the arrest came as a surprise – “I was confused! Did I speed?” he thought – Chambers revealed to the Guardian that a car had been following him around Dublin only days before, and that someone had broken into their car parked outside their house at night, without taking anything of value.
“I noticed signs of surveillance,” he said. Months later, last Wednesday, Irish police raided the same house, acting on a request from US authorities.
With his immediate future uncertain, Chambers said he was “looking forward to sharing a couple of nice dinners with my family this week”.
As for the past, he said the millions he has donated to an estimated 100 projects in about 20 countries is “the most important thing I’ve done”.

“Somebody with the political orientation I have and with resources, no matter how good of an activist I am, it’s not gonna be as effective as medical aid or feeding children in Gaza, supporting independent media that wouldn’t otherwise exist, or paying people’s bail who have been arrested for protesting.
“I’m giving a lot of money to things that other people aren’t giving money to.”
Chambers also said he was “grateful for the way Spanish courts have dealt with this – just focusing on the facts. It shouldn’t matter that I’ve made some emotional statements.”

articles.title: DOJ vows to fast-track release of eligible PDLs aged 70 and up
articles.summary: The Department of Justice (DOJ) on Wednesday committed to expedite the release of eligible persons deprived of liberty (PDLs) aged 70 and above as part of efforts to decongest jails.

blocks.text: Published November 25, 2026 6:51pm
The Department of Justice (DOJ) on Wednesday committed to expedite the release of eligible persons deprived of liberty (PDLs) aged 70 and above as part of efforts to decongest jails.
Budget sponsor Senator Francis “Kiko” Pangilinan said this during the Senate plenary deliberations into the proposed P44.283 billion budget of the DOJ and its attached agencies for fiscal year 2027.

“According to the good Secretary, this December 7, the Executive — Office of the President through the Deputy Executive Secretary for Legal Affairs — will be precisely discussing how to fast-track the procedure and to discuss those pending matters for release with the OP,” Pangilinan said.
This came after Senator Imee Marcos appealed to fast-track the release of PDLs who are already very old and have served their sentences for many years.
Eligibility

“Pakiusap na lamang ito na palayain ang mga lola. Dahil alam naman natin kapag 'yung PDL ay 70 years old or older and has served 10 years, 22 years, 'yung iba sa kanila higit pa, they are primarily eligible for executive clemency, hindi na regular parole,” Marcos said.

(Please just release the elderly PDLs. We know that when the PDL is 70 years old or older and has served 10 years, 22 years, some of them even more, they are primarily eligible for executive clemency, not regular parole.)

“We are all very clear that the age and the time served, the high risk status which is no longer extant even if they were convicted of a heinous crime, at that advanced age they are absolutely no threat to society,” she added.

Marcos cited Malacañang’s Memorandum Order No. 155, directing the Bureau of Corrections (BuCor), Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP), and the Board of Pardons and Parole (BPP) to immediately forward to the Office of the President records of inmates who are 70 years and above and are serving sentence by final judgment in order that the same may be considered for the purpose of extending executive clemency.

The agencies were also ordered to automatically submit names of inmates turning 70 years old and to transmit records of the said inmates to the Office of the President for review of their eligibility for executive clemency.
The senator also said the elderly PDLs could avail of the good conduct time allowance under the under Republic Act No. 10592.
Holidays

“Sana habulin na natin. December na po, Pasko na. Panahon na talaga para sa executive clemency. 'Yun lang ang hinihiling ko kasi kung tutuusin, lumalabag rin tayo sa batas sa kaka-delay nang kaka-delay,” Marcos said.

(I hope we can catch up now. It’s already December, it’s Christmas soon. It really is time for executive clemency. That is all I am asking for, because, honestly, we are actually violating the law ourselves by constantly delaying this.)

“They are really qualified and deserving. Marami sa kanila may (many of them have) terminal cancer and other illnesses — they are already wheelchair-bound, and they have families and institutions perfectly happy to take care of them,” she continued.
Citing data from DOJ, Pangilinan said the number of PDLs being released has increased since 2020.
“In 2024, halos 100% ang dumoble na ang mga releases from 2020. In 2025, about, from 57,000, they released 75,000---that's about 50% more,” the budget sponsor said.
(In 2024, the releases reached almost 100%, double the figures from 2020. In 2025, from 57,000, they released 75,000---that's about 50% more.)
“So dumadami na ang number of PDLs being released (so the number of PDLs being released is increasing). The rate has increased, but yes, they still need to do it faster,” he added. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Bill to teach students Critical Media and Info Literacy aims to counter fake news
articles.summary: A bill requiring a Critical Media and Information Literacy subject across all levels of the Philippine educational system has been filed in the House of Representatives.

blocks.text: Published November 25, 2026 6:33pm
A bill requiring a Critical Media and Information Literacy subject across all levels of the Philippine educational system has been filed in the House of Representatives.
House Deputy Minority Leader Antonio Tinio of ACT Teachers party-list and Representatives Sarah Elago of Gabriela and Renee Co of Kabataan made the proposal under House Bill 12061.

The authors said that the Critical Media and Information Literacy subject would cover topics beyond basic technical or analytical skills and critical media literacy, and involves an ideological critique of media representations, an analysis of power dynamics underpinning information control, and the activeproduction of alternative media.

The authors said the measure is urgent given that information is now easily digested through posts, tweets, and videos seen in various social media platforms, a situation that has led to the democratization of information production and dissemination—but also one that can be controlled by powerful political and economic actors to systematically manufacture public consent and distort reality at the same time.

“There is a prevalence of Al-generated content, in which individuals can freely alter data, structure its legitimacy, imitating information produced by authorized media institutions. Without thorough assessment and fact-checking, it is no longer unacceptable to say that the public is exposed to a wide variety of news, the truthfulness of which ranging from most reliable to most questionable,” the bill read.

The lawmakers said the advent of sophisticated artificial intelligence (AI) tools has also exponentially increased the scale and believability of fabricated content, from deepfake videos to Al-generated news articles, creating an environment where distinguishing fact from malicious fiction requires advanced analytical skills.

“This bill seeks to transform Filipino students from passive recipients of information into empowered, critical citizens capable of defending democratic discourse from manipulation and fostering a culture of truth-seeking and civic engagement,” the bill added.
Co, for her part, said the subject will train students to go beyond memorization and sharpen comprehension.
"Dapat sanayin ang bawat estudyante na kumwestiyon, mag-imbestiga, at sumalungat sa kasinungalingan. Huwag tayo basta na lang mag-scroll at maniwala sa kung ano ang nakikita sa screen," Co said.
(We should train our students to ask questions, investigate and fight lies. We must learn not to simply scroll and believe everything we see online.)
"Pag mulat at kritikal ang kabataan, hindi sila basta-basta mabubudol ng mga fake news peddlers. Sila mismo ang magiging bantay ng katotohanan at demokrasya," she added.
(If the students are aware and critical, they won't easily fall to fake news peddlers. Instead, they will be the guardrails of truth and democracy.)
— BM, GMA News
Follow facebook.com/gmanewsonline for real-time news and developments in the Philippines and around the world.

articles.title: Protesters call on Israel to free Palestinian student held without charge
articles.summary: Mahdi Tunsi, 26, was taken from his university dormitory earlier this month and has since been held without charge.

blocks.text: Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images
Mahdi Tunsi appears by videolink in front of his attorney Nasser Odeh during his hearing at the Jerusalem District Court on Tuesday
ByKaty Watson
Reporting fromEast Jerusalem

Israeli students, activists and academics are calling for the release of a Palestinian undergraduate who was taken from his university dormitory by Israeli police earlier this month and has since been held without charge.
Mahdi Tunsi, a 26-year-old sociology and criminology student at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, appeared in an Israeli court in the city on Tuesday - a hearing that was held behind closed doors.
Israeli police say he was arrested "concerning ties to an act of terrorism".

Authorities have requested what is known as "administrative detention", which allows the Israeli state to detain people indefinitely without charge on the basis of secret evidence that they cannot see.
"We definitely think this is a political arrest," said Dr Yael Berda, one of Tunsi's university professors.

Tunsi, a Palestinian resident of occupied East Jerusalem who works with well-known Jewish-Palestinian campaign groups, was arrested a month after Israel held an election that saw Arab-led parties win a record 19 seats in parliament, the Knesset, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing coalition lose its majority.
Since then, Berda said she had seen an intensifying campaign against Palestinian rights.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Knesset Member Dr Ofer Cassif was one of the those gathered outside the court

blocks.text: Knesset Member Dr Ofer Cassif was one of the those gathered outside the court
Outside the Jerusalem District Court on Tuesday, demonstrators waved placards with a black-and-white image of Tunsi, while crying out "shame" in unison.

"There's no due process - [administrative detention is] a sugar-coated term for being kidnapped and held as a hostage," said Dr Ofer Cassif, a Member of the Knesset representing the Arab-led Joint List alliance.
"We must all stand firm against such crimes. It's unacceptable."
Since the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, which triggered the Gaza war, the number of people in administrative detention has more than doubled.

In October, there were more than 3,100 in administrative detention, according to Israel Prison Service figures published by Israeli rights group HaMoked. Most of them are Palestinians from the occupied West Bank.
Israel says that its use of the policy is compliant with international law and a necessary preventative measure to combat terrorism.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Protesters held signs calling for Tunsi to be freed in Arabic and Hebrew

blocks.text: Protesters held signs calling for Tunsi to be freed in Arabic and Hebrew
In a statement, Israeli police said they would "not elaborate further regarding the investigation" into Tunsi.

He appeared via video link from prison - his hair and beard shaved off. His friends also said that he was without medication as well as his glasses, despite a judge requesting them to be brought to him in detention.
The Israel Prison Service said it acted in accordance with the court's rulings.

"When the process was complete and all the necessary approvals had been received, the detainee's lawyer was told he could pass the eyeglasses to the detainee immediately, subject to security procedures," it added.
Berda asked to enter the courtroom on Tuesday but was denied entry. According to Berda, not even Tunsi has been told of the evidence against him.
The judge has said more time is needed to consider the state's request for administrative detention. A decision is expected in the coming days.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The judge has said more time is needed to consider the state's request for administrative detention

blocks.text: The judge has said more time is needed to consider the state's request for administrative detention
"If they have evidence, have them bring it or release him," said Berda.
"That's why we're demanding his immediate release or moving it to a criminal track where he could defend himself."
Berda said that while Tunsi could not vote in Israel's general election because he is not an Israeli citizen, he was "engaged" and very supportive of Arab parties' involvement.
"Mahdi is one of the best human beings I know," said Noga Kaplan, who studies with him at the Hebrew University.
"He has a really pure heart and is very passionate about his studies."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Protesters demand the release of Mahdi Tunsi outside the Jerusalem Central Court during his hearing.

blocks.text: Protesters demand the release of Mahdi Tunsi outside the Jerusalem Central Court during his hearing.
After Tunsi's arrest, the Hebrew University issued a statement saying it was notified a few minutes before it took place.

"The university is not a party to the legal proceedings involving the student, and we do not have information that would allow us to comment on the circumstances leading to the arrest or on the ongoing legal proceedings," it said.
It added that it was concerned for Tunsi's well-being and hoped "that the matter will be resolved promptly and that his rights will be fully respected throughout the process".

Tunsi is a resident of Silwan, a neighbourhood in East Jerusalem where, in recent years, Palestinians have been evicted by Israeli authorities, who say their properties were built illegally. Israeli settlers have since moved into some of those properties.
"Political organisation stopped after October 7 because people were getting super scared about the consequences," explained Kaplan.
"Mahdi saw studying as one of the ways to speak about it in class."
"He didn't do a lot of public stuff because what's happening now is his biggest fear."

articles.title: Colombian police storm supermarket to free 20 held hostage for 17 hours
articles.summary: One gunman was killed in the operation to free around 20 shoppers and employees after a 17-hour hostage ordeal.

blocks.text: Residents living near the supermarket reported hearing explosions as the security forces moved into the building.
Police later confirmed that officers had used stun grenades to overpower the hostage takers.
De la Espriella described it as "an extraordinary joint operation", which he said had been carried out "flawlessly".
He flew into the northern city to oversee the operation.
In footage released since then, he can be seen speaking into a walkie-talkie and carrying a handgun strapped to his side.
Speaking after the successful rescue of the hostages, he said that the gunmen had been given the chance to hand themselves in, which they had refused.
Earlier in the day, the men had freed 10 of their hostages, among them elderly women.
But they continued to hold around 20, even as a police helicopter hovered above and special forces erected a perimeter around the building.
Local media said that as well as demanding safe passage out of the supermarket, the gunmen also demanded nearly $2m (£1.5m) and armoured vehicles.
According to President De la Espriella, they had no political affiliations but had taken the hostages once their plan to rob an armoured car carrying money had been foiled.
"It's not that a terrorist group carried out a kidnapping - no, these are criminals who were caught off guard, had no way out, and then kidnapped a group of people," he said.
Photos taken during the rescue operation show armed soldiers inside the building while people are kneeling with their hands behind their heads.

articles.title: Climate loss and damage fund exists, but the money doesn't
articles.summary: Climate-vulnerable countries fought for years to create a loss and damage fund. Four years on, demand far outstrips funding, pledges are scarce, and disaster-hit nations are still waiting for support.

image.caption: Nepal in the aftermath of August flash floods that killed more than 1,500 people, with thousands more missingImage: Arun Sankar/AFP

blocks.text: On the sandbars and river islands of Bangladesh's Brahmaputra and its branches, families have little to fall back on when the water rises.
"The floodwater swallows everything," said 16-year-old Rasel Babu who had traveled to Antalya, Turkey to speak to delegates at the UN climate conference.

Created after years of pressure from vulnerable nations, the loss and damage fund was designed to help countries recover from climate disasters and irreversible climate impacts. This includes extreme weather events such as floods, heat waves and wildfires as well as slow onset impacts such as sea level rise, desertification and damage to infrastructure and crops.
But the fund is already struggling to meet demand. It received $2.8 billion (€2.56 billion) in urgent requests in a first call for funding, with only $342 million available at the time.
Even the money promised has not fully arrived. Only about half of the money currently pledged had been received by this summer.

While the European Commission signed a €25 million ($27 million) contribution agreement to the fund on the margins of COP31, formalizing an earlier pledge made at COP28, and Spain pledged an additional €15 million, other contributions to loss and damage remained scarce.
First payout will go to Nepal after glacier collapse

The fund's first emergency response is going to be paid out to Nepal. The board of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage had provisionally set aside $21.6 million following the catastrophic glacier collapse that triggered flash floods in August, killing more than 1,500 people with 5,600 more missing.
But the money has not moved yet. Nepal must first submit a funding request setting out how it will be spent.

"It's asking for a country that is dealing with the climate emergency to work on a proposal," Nepali climate finance expert Bibek Raj Kandel said, adding a layer of bureaucracy inefficient to address the urgency.
UN warns climate change could force millions to move

Nepal is already waiting on another request, filed after floods in Kathmandu and landslides in the eastern hills. "There's already one pending proposal sitting on the table," Kandel said. Unless the fund speeds up, he warned, it's "going to disappoint many, many countries."
Pakistan which led the push for the fund in 2022 after floods affected 33 million people and killed more than 1,730, also hasn't seen any of the money yet.

"Pakistan was one of the countries which really spoke up and managed to get the loss and damage fund on the climate agenda. But it takes a long time," Pakistan's Minister of State for Climate Change, Shezra Mansab Ali Khan Kharal, told DW.

blocks.caption: In 2022, monsoon and floods killed more than 1,730 people in Pakistan, with 33 million people affectedImage: Akhtar Soomro/REUTERS

blocks.text: "We have still not really got anything. We haven't seen anything on the ground at all as yet," Kharal said. Pakistan has submitted two projects and was told the cap is $200 million.
Other forms of aid often come in the form of loans.

"These promises, they are hollow promises," said Abid Qaiyum Suleri, Executive Director of the Sustainable Development Policy Institute (SDPI) in Islamabad, adding that for a heavily indebted country, the form of the money matters as much as the amount.
"We do not want that a climate disaster in Pakistan should translate into further debt for Pakistan," Kharal said, calling for grants rather than loans.

articles.title: Germany's women's football team take stand against domestic violence
articles.summary: Germany's women's football team are to wear UN Women badges in games against Argentina and Peru, as domestic violence hits a record high in Germany.

image.caption: Germany's women have been strong supporters of the campaign, as the orange logo of 'stop violence agianst women' reveals on Lea Schüller's sleeveImage: imago images/Beautiful Sports

blocks.text: Domestic violence has reached a record high in Germany, with 16 women subjected to physical abuse behind closed doors each hour.

UN Women Germany is one of 13 UN Women national committees worldwide, each an independent, non-profit, non-governmental organization committed to gender equality and the empowerment of women and girls.

Their current campaign "Orange The World" runs from the start of International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women on November 25 to December 10, International Human Rights Day. It is designed to raise awareness around violence against women in the country and worldwide. The 2026 campaign's focus is particularly on men's responsibility in ending gender-based violence.

"In these 16 days of activism, we can deliver a lot of information. Survivors of gender-based violence can find out where to get support and be reminded that they are not at fault," UN Women Germany chair, politician and long-standing campaigner for women's rights Elke Ferner told DW. "The debate helps and it's a chance to change consciousness about the topic."

Germany captain Giulia Gwinn said in a statement via the German Football Association (DFB): "Violence against women and girls affects us all and must have no place in our society. As the women's national team, we therefore want to once again use our reach to create awareness for this important issue and jointly set a visible sign against violence."
The campaign with the women's team is not new. Two years ago, the team joined the campaign, delivering a moving video that saw players reveal the truth of statements by crossing out words.

During Germany's upcoming South America tour — part of their preparations for the 2027 World Cup in Brazil — they are to wear special UN Women Germany badges on their sleeves in their games against Argentina and Peru.
Role models pivotal for the campaign

Ferner believes the work with role models is pivotal and that the campaign is powerful, especially in a football context. A 2022 study from Warwick Business School in the UK revealed alcohol-related domestic abuse rises by nearly 50% after England's men's football team win a World Cup game, never mind lose.

Currently, there is no data on domestic abuse during Germany games, however during the 2026 World Cup last summer, Berlin police recorded a 31% increase in domestic violence compared to the week before.

Ferner is encouraged that sport has understood the importance of the issue, and that the German Olympic Committee (DOSB) and other sports clubs and organizations are helping move the conversation forward.

In sport, this is particularly important given the problematic nature of dependency relationships that so often exist in high-performance environments. But violence against women is really a societal issue that is not specific to class, origin, religion or societal space, such as sport.

"Violence against women has structural origins and to change that you need to change the structures," Ferner said. "You just need to do it. I always say, this isn't about a lack of knowledge but rather a lack of action."
Performance is an integral part of sport, but a multi-dimensional understanding of it might help shift perspective in a country that remains driven by a performance culture.

"What is performance? Higher, faster, further? Or is it managing to look after a family of three?" Ferner asked. "Why do people who repair washing machines earn more than those looking after your kids in nursery? This is about changing business culture, but also awareness around the role men play at home and in the family.

"The picture boys and young men get of girls and women in school is a problem that needs addressing. We can't wait for generational change. This is about saving lives. We need to change societal structures."
Male power structures a problem

Sports structures are also in need of reform. Non-profit organization Safe Sport provides independent support for people affected by sexual, physical and psychological violence in both amateur and professional sport in Germany.

They are the only organization with a specific focus on violence in grassroots sports in Germany, and one of only two in professional sport in the country. They also have to contend with structures, in a sporting context, that make spaces less safe for women.

"Gender roles have become more fluid in the last few years, but in associations and clubs management positions are still occupied by men, regardless of the sport," Safe Sport manager Ina Lambert told DW.
"In professional sport, there are a lot fewer women involved in training and so the space remains male dominated, and, as a result, so do the power structures.

"We have people in search of advice, men included, who see the problems and want to enforce change, and we offer them support so they are not alone," Lambert said. "But whether in a big association or a small club, perpetrators are frequently protected, incidents are ignored and so the people who want to enforce change are often prevented from doing so."

Safe Sport, which provides free psychological and legal support, has only been in action since July 2023, but in that time the number of support requests they have received continues to grow. Psychological violence in sport in Germany is the most common case they are faced with, but sexual violence is also a major problem.
"There is finally recognition of the problem and there is a seriousness about tackling it," Lambert said.

"There is a lot of good work being done in the right direction, with many good concepts for prevention, intervention and processing violence, as well as more education, holistic training and focus on women's menstrual cycles."

blocks.caption: Germany is backing UN efforts to highlight that more must be done to tackle violence against womenImage: imago images/Lucca Fundel

blocks.text: Comprehensive support on the way

Germany's Interior Ministry is leading the process with participants from the country's states, organized sport, affected parties and academia to create a central hub. The center for safe sport was founded in July 2026, but investigative and sanctioning work is expected to begin in the spring of 2027.
Support from leading figures clearly makes a huge difference, but it's also clear that more data is needed. Addressing the underlying issues, such as social norms and gender stereotyping, is a must.

After all, as UN Women Executive Director Sima Bahous said: "No country has yet eliminated violence against women. Ending it requires transformative action — greater investment, innovation, and unwavering political will."
This article was originally published on November 28, 2024, and updated on November 25, 2026.

articles.title: All hostages rescued after Colombian security forces storm supermarket, says president
articles.summary:
Operation in which one hostage-taker was killed ends daylong siege in Cartegena shopping centre, where 30 people were initially held

Colombian security forces have stormed a supermarket in…

blocks.text: Colombian security forces have stormed a supermarket in the Caribbean city of Cartagena, ending a daylong hostage siege, with the president saying all those held had been rescued and one hostage-taker killed.
Several explosions were heard before security forces entered the building, where about 20 people were believed to be being held by armed men.
President Abelardo de la Espriella, said: “In an extraordinary joint operation between the national police and the armed forces, all the hostages were rescued.”

Shortly after midnight on Wednesday, a police helicopter was hovering low over the shopping centre as security forces massed outside the supermarket. Explosions then echoed around the complex as tactical teams moved in.
Ten of an estimated 30 people that were initially held had already been released during the 17-hour standoff, including several elderly women.
Moments later, soldiers could be seen inside the Éxito supermarket as security forces secured the building.

De la Espriella, who appeared at the scene wearing fatigues and carrying a sidearm and a walkie-talkie, described the operation as a success. He said: “We gave them the opportunity to surrender and free the hostages. They rejected that opportunity and we acted decisively.”
Cartagena’s mayor said all the hostages were “safe and sound” and would be reunited with their families before undergoing medical checks.
The siege gripped Cartagena, a Caribbean port famed for its colonial walled old town, beach resorts and cruise-ship tourism. Supermarket employees had been among those feared trapped inside.

blocks.caption: Hostages inside the supermarket. Photograph: Sergio Jimenez Ciro/EPA

blocks.text: “My son is there,” Jacob Pérez, the father of one of the workers, said earlier in the standoff. “He didn’t leave work and he’s not answering his phone. I think they took it from him.”
Images broadcast by Colombian media and shared online appeared to show masked gunmen in tactical gear alongside zip-tied hostages inside the store.

De la Espriella was quick to rule out the involvement of guerrilla or paramilitary groups. “It’s not that a terrorist group carried out a kidnapping – no, these are criminals who were caught off guard, had no way out, and then kidnapped a group of people,” he said.
Authorities said the siege began after an attempted robbery on an armoured vehicle at the shopping centre.

According to local media, the hostage-takers were demanding nearly US$2m (£1.5m), two armoured vehicles and safe passage to the city of Barranquilla, about 80 miles (130km) north-east of Cartagena. AFP could not independently verify those reports.

The siege began on the 10th anniversary of Colombia’s landmark peace accord with Farc guerrillas amid a series of attacks across the country. Despite the deal to end the region’s largest insurgency, dissident guerrilla groups and criminal organisations still fight for control of parts of the country.
On Monday, authorities blamed a dissident Farc faction for a car bomb attack in the city of Villavicencio that wounded 25 people and caused extensive damage.

Separately, the presidency said a “terrorist attack” on electrical infrastructure had disrupted power supplies in several south-western departments and prompted additional measures to protect energy facilities.

articles.title: ‘Russia wants more than Ukraine,’ Germany’s Merz warns – Europe live
articles.summary:
German chancellor, in wide-ranging speech, says Moscow is ‘escalating on a massive scale’

Merz also touches on this week’s EU summit, starting tomorrow, and the likely…

blocks.text: 'Russia wants more than Ukraine,' Germany's Merz warns, as he says Moscow is 'escalating on a massive scale'

In his wide-ranging budget speech, Merz talks about Germany “neglecting fundamental issues for far too long” on defence, infrastructure, demographic change, and the economy – and the need to address these issues urgently.
But the starkest part of his speech comes as he talks about the external situation – and particularly the threat from Russia - to explain why some decisions, particularly on defence, are needed.
“Russia knows exactly what it wants and Russia wants more than Ukraine,” he warns.

“Anyone who fails to grasp this either does not understand the world as it is, or is pursuing an entirely different agenda – one that stands in opposition to the freedom, openness, and liberal values ​​of our own country.”
Merz warns that “Russia is escalating tensions in the Baltic region, in Poland, in the Black Sea, and even in the outer space.”

“It is escalating on a massive scale – including here within our own borders, even at the cost of human lives. That is the situation, ladies and gentlemen. And that is why we, as Europeans, must—and will – set clear boundaries for Russia.”
Key events

items: 14m agoGermany has 'begun to change course' amid major challenges, Merz says
22m ago'By supporting Ukraine, we are supporting and protecting ourselves,' Merz tells parliament
26m ago'Russia wants more than Ukraine,' Germany's Merz warns, as he says Moscow is 'escalating on a massive scale'
37m agoMorning opening: Ukraine reporting energy outages in five regions after Russian strikes

blocks.text: Germany has 'begun to change course' amid major challenges, Merz says
Merz also touches on this week’s EU summit, starting tomorrow, and the likely contentious negotiations over the next EU budget.
He pushes back on “impressions” that he thinks Germany spends too much on EU contributions.
But he says he is “pushing for us to limit and focus our spending on what truly strengthens Europe today,” specifically on security and competitiveness.

In a pretty passionate defence of European integration, he says only such focused spending will give Europe “an assurance that we will not simply become a plaything in this world, but have a hand in shaping it.”

Summing up, he repeats his earlier point that Germany faces major challenges that have been unresolved for too long, and so one budget “is far from solving all of our problems,” but says “we have begun to change course” as economic indicators are starting to improve.
And he ends his speech there.

blocks.caption: German chancellor Friedrich Merz takes a drink of water as he sits down after his speech. Photograph: Odd Andersen/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: 'By supporting Ukraine, we are supporting and protecting ourselves,' Merz tells parliament

Merz goes back to last week’s meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Berlin, saying the US delegation was “it seemed to me, quite clearly surprised by how united … the Europeans are on this issue.”
“It is precisely this determination, ladies and gentlemen, that allows for a cautious optimism regarding the prospect of peace – a genuine peace,” he says.
He keeps coming back to his main message: “by supporting Ukraine, we are supporting and protecting ourselves.”
“This is true in a sense that may not yet be fully understood by many in our country,” he stresses.
Germany’s chancellor Friedrich Merz is speaking in the Bundestag now – mostly on the 2027 budget, but he’s also touching upon broader issues, including on Russia and Ukraine.

blocks.caption: German chancellor Friedrich Merz speaks on the day of the 2027 budget debate at the German lower house of parliament, the Bundestag, in Berlin. Photograph: Liesa Johannssen/Reuters

blocks.text: I will bring you key quotes here.
Morning opening: Ukraine reporting energy outages in five regions after Russian strikes

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa
Russian strikes ⁠on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure overnight caused ⁠power ⁠outages in ​five regions, deputy energy minister ⁠Artem Nekrasov said this morning.

blocks.caption: Local residents stand outside a damaged residential building following a Russian air strike that killed two and wounded another 40 in the centre of Zaporizhzhia yesterday. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The ⁠affected regions are ​Dnipropetrovsk, ‌Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Odesa ‌and Kharkiv. The ‌situation is most difficult in the Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk regions, he said, as reported by Reuters.
Separately, at least two people were killed in a strike in Odesa, and injuries were reported in Kyiv after a strike on a multi-storey apartment in the capital.
The latest attacks come just hours before Nato’s secretary general Mark Rutte is due to meet with the US president, Donald Trump, in Mar-A-Lago for talks behind the closed doors.
Their meeting comes amid reported delays in air defence missile deliveries to Ukraine, as the country braces for a tough winter under continuing Russian assaults.
I will bring you all the latest here.
It’s Wednesday, 25 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.

articles.title: Large bushfire threatens homes and properties on remote island off Tasmania
articles.summary:
Blaze spreads significantly across the north of Flinders Island after being started by lightning strikes

  • Get our

blocks.text: Homes and properties on a picturesque remote island are under threat from an out-of-control bushfire that has sent smoke hundreds of kilometres south.
The blaze on Flinders Island in Bass Strait spread significantly on Wednesday after being started by lightning strikes.
Some structures had been destroyed but it was too early to tell whether they were homes, the Tasmania Fire Service incident controller Steven Richardson said.
A Bureau of Meteorology post on X featured a video showing a vast column of smoke being blown south across north-east Tasmania, as northerly winds pushed the plume across Bass Strait.

blocks.caption: Authorities said it was too early to tell whether any homes had been lost in the blaze.  Photograph: Tasmania Fire Service

blocks.text: As of Wednesday night, three emergency warnings were in place, including for the coastal settlement of Killiecrankie and nearby areas Leeka, Mount Tanner, Mount Boyes and Carnacs Flat.
Some residents were warned it was too late to leave.
Roughly 3,000 hectares had been burned by the fire on Tuesday, before it spread south on Wednesday following a wind change.
Residents on the island, which is about 130,000 hectares in size and home to 900 people, posted photos of massive plumes of smoke on social media.
Mick Grimshaw, a farmer, helped friends move cattle from their property and said they had lost some fences.
“We were under the ashes. Right there. But we’ve got them safe,” he told ABC radio.
“The fire threat for this farm looks like it has abated a bit but certainly not further down the island.
“We can see the smoke front heading right down the guts of the island.”
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: A ringtail possum near the burnt-out bush on Flinders Island. Photograph: Tasmania Fire Service

blocks.text: Nearly 40 firefighters were working to control the bushfire, plus 12 parks and wildlife staff, five helicopters and three aircraft.
“Additional resources are being deployed and Tasmania Police is also helping evacuate people, particularly in the Leeka and Mount Tanner areas,” parks minister Nick Duigan said.
“There is a lot of smoke in the area and it’s now coming down Tasmania’s coast.”
Several roads have been closed because of poor visibility due to smoke.
Flinders Island is known for high-quality exports, including beef, lamb, wool and seafood.
